0066daed-f170-56db-b502-467e8b3e136c.name: Italian Company Breda Ernesto. Factory for Torpedoes and Navy Equipment, Milan. View of the Female Section of Lathes Division. Production of 75 mm Shrapnel Shells
0066daed-f170-56db-b502-467e8b3e136c.author: Cristina Mosillo, Giulia Barrera
0066daed-f170-56db-b502-467e8b3e136c.archival: ACS, Ministero armi e munizioni, Ufficio storiografico della mobilitazione civile e industriale, Archivio fotografico, fasc. 148, foto 2039, neg. 2195 B.
0066daed-f170-56db-b502-467e8b3e136c.third_name: Soc. Italiana Breda Ernesto. Stabilimento per siluri e lavori di marina, Milano. Veduta  del reparto femminile della torneria. Lavorazione degli shrapnels da 75 mm.
0066daed-f170-56db-b502-467e8b3e136c.second_name: Women working in a factory that produced military equipment, during World War I
0066daed-f170-56db-b502-467e8b3e136c.description2:
Women working at lathes to make shrapnel shells in an Italian factory that produced torpedoes and other weapons. The war had an important impact on women’s work.  
As historian Perry Willson pointed out, during WWI “women rarely directly substituted for men, instead tending to move into new work roles produced by wartime expansion.”  
In Italy, the number of women who worked in factories producing weapons and ammunitions rose from 23,000 in 1915 to 198,000 in 1918. The numbers were far less than the women who participated in war production with more traditional “female roles”, such as making uniforms (400,000) or knitting woollen garments for the soldiers (200,000). However, Willson explained, women working in weapons’ factories had a relevance “as symbolic harbinger of change that greatly outweighed their actual numbers.”

en: Willson, Perry R., *Women in Twentieth-century Italy*, New York: Palgrave Macmillan, 2010.

0b0283d8-2b68-513e-ac6c-83c7af076357.name: *Street scribe*
0b0283d8-2b68-513e-ac6c-83c7af076357.description:
This illustration is included in a book written by James Augustus Saint John, a British writer and traveller who visited Egypt and Nubia in 1832 and published a book about the places and people he had seen. The author focused on details aiming at illustrating (according to his point of view) the life of the country.  
  
This illustration of a street scribe shows how traditional jobs were still active in Egyptian society at a time when the country was undergoing political, social and administrative changes under Muhammad ‘Ali Pasha. The illustration suggests an unintentional comparison with European countries at that time, where although social, political and technical changes were also happening, urban and rural society continued to retain traditional jobs like the street scribe.

0b5e2b9b-6dd4-501c-9d61-0af91a0c8de8.name: 5 May 1919, bank employees on strike [at the trade unions building,  Rue de la Grange-aux-Belles, 10e arrondissement, Paris.
0b5e2b9b-6dd4-501c-9d61-0af91a0c8de8.description2: The difficulties in returning to peacetime society after the end of the First World War created huge shifts in the social fabric of Paris. The city saw continuous strikes from May to July 1919. The most numerically significant was the steelworkers' strike, but all sectors were affected, as we can see from this photo, in which bank workers protest the "high cost of living" and "insufficient salaries".

Silver jewellery was the most common because only rich people could afford gold jewellery. Silver or gold jewellery was part of the dowry given by the groom to the bride. The material (gold or silver) and even the coins used as pieces of jewellery were an indirect statement of the financial status of the groom.

0d4f3f4b-f17c-5cc6-86eb-8f3f56c416b7.name: Madrasa al-Bachiya
0d4f3f4b-f17c-5cc6-86eb-8f3f56c416b7.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
0d4f3f4b-f17c-5cc6-86eb-8f3f56c416b7.history: The *madrasa* was the accommodation building for the students of the Zaytuna University. The students lived in rooms resembling monastic cells around an open-air courtyard surrounded by covered porticos, and were able to both study and pray here.
0d4f3f4b-f17c-5cc6-86eb-8f3f56c416b7.description2: Located in the Suq des Libraires, this *madrasa* was built by 'Ali Pacha, the nephew Hussein ben 'Ali. It was built in the mid-18th century in the standard style of the time, distinguished only by its rich plaster décor and ceramic tiles, a *tourba* (funerary vault) for the builder and his family attached to the building, and a *sabil* (water fountain) for public use. Today, the *madrasa* has become a training centre for a crafts and apprenticeship college.

0dc23a30-fb0c-549b-b031-54f5fa9e9a23.description2: Pictured here is the dormitory of 'Ayntura school, a large rectangular room with a high ceiling, supported by tall, thin columns. The room has several windows and is furnished with identical wooden beds.

0fa95d00-46ca-5bec-8348-9b86a0617d78.description2: On obverse *tuğra* of sultan Abdul Hamid II, flower to right, denomination below: ١٠ ش “10 sh”, all within wreath with crossed quivers and unstrung bow at bottom, above seven stars, “W” below wreath tie. On reverse: within a wreath: “*duriba fi misr* 1293 22” (“22, struck in Misr, 1293”). Above 3 stars. It was issued in the year 22 (AH 1317 / AD 1896) of sultan Abdul Hamid II’s reign (Hegira 1293–1327 / AD 1876–1909).

1028751a-07f0-53c2-8d14-e1b298d6e008.name: Board
1028751a-07f0-53c2-8d14-e1b298d6e008.description: Qur'anic board used in the African *madrasas* (schools), places where the first verses of the Qur'an are learned, under the direction of the *marabout* (teacher). The learning method consists of copying and reciting the different verses of the Qur'an, in a process of memorisation, which allows the students to erase them and then to write the following verses. The *alluha* (table of wood), the reed, and the ink are the only available pedagogic materials of the Qur'anic schools in the rural areas. The Qur'anic boards turn into documents that preserve the written personality of those who used them, the irregularity of the letter, the crooked lines, the hesitations, the corrected mistakes, the erased lines that refuse to disappear, as a register of a period of effort and domain of skills typical of the school stage.

10a5b375-34b0-5c68-bd08-21bc738e5e36.name: Lisbon Botanical Garden
10a5b375-34b0-5c68-bd08-21bc738e5e36.type: Botanical Garden; National Monument (Decree nº18/2010, DR, nº250  28  December 2010)
10a5b375-34b0-5c68-bd08-21bc738e5e36.holder: National Museum of Natural History and Science (MUHNAC) / Museums of the University of Lisbon
10a5b375-34b0-5c68-bd08-21bc738e5e36.dates: Starting of plantation: 1873; opened to the public: 1878; belongs to the University of Lisbon since 1911
10a5b375-34b0-5c68-bd08-21bc738e5e36.author: Catarina Teixeira (MUHNAC-UL), David Felismino (MUHNAC-UL)
10a5b375-34b0-5c68-bd08-21bc738e5e36.history: Since its creation in 1837, the Polytechnic School is committed to use  the Botanical Garden to support teaching and research in Botany. This purpose was firstly achieved at the Royal Botanical Garden at Ajuda, whose scientific and administrative supervision passed to the Polytechnic School in 1839. The installation of the new garden begins in 1873, on the initiative of Conde de Ficalho (1837–1903), and it opens to the public in 1878. In the 20th century, a new Herbarium building was added (1942) and, in 1962, a new Greenhouse replacing the original one, degraded by use and by the bombings of 1927. Topographically the Botanic Garden consists of two distinct parts – a flat area, dedicated to systematic botany and a gentle slope with the collection of trees and shrubs (Arboretum).
10a5b375-34b0-5c68-bd08-21bc738e5e36.keywords: Botanical Garden; Collections; National Museum of Natural History and Science; Polytechnic School
10a5b375-34b0-5c68-bd08-21bc738e5e36.architects: Ordered by Manuel Melo Breyner, Conde de Ficalho (1837–1903). Author of the design and arrangement of the Order Beds: German botanist Goeze Edmund (1838–1929), Arboretum: French botanist Jules Daveau (1852–1929)
10a5b375-34b0-5c68-bd08-21bc738e5e36.second_name: Botanical Garden of the University of Lisbon
10a5b375-34b0-5c68-bd08-21bc738e5e36.description2: The Garden holds more than 1,500 specimens over 4 acres, highlighting a remarkable diversity of palms and a unique collection of Cycadaceae, with exemplars only surviving in some parts of the world. It is also rich in species from New Zealand, Australia, China, Japan and South America, demonstrating the peculiarities of different microclimates created by its topography. The Garden fulfils also national requirements, both by the universality of its collection, and by the quality and quantity of the associated collections (herbaria, wood collections, seed bank). Furthermore, it includes relevant edified heritage, designed by important Portuguese architects from the 19th and 20th centuries.

11568132-d5af-54cf-9a3f-f663abfb4f5b.description2: Sleeveless jacket made of woollen fabric of red and black stripes, decorated with floral motifs of orange and purple colour with couching in silk threads on the shoulders and the bottom. This object illustrates the variegated population composition of the Jordanian territory in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, influenced by the local economy. The main activities were trade and crafts that influenced population movements and the coexistence of various local and foreign communities.

12e1f5c3-c135-5c06-b2c9-4dc99c6e764e.name: Clashes between agricultural labourers on strike and the mounted police in Cerignola (Foggia, Apulia, in southern Italy)
12e1f5c3-c135-5c06-b2c9-4dc99c6e764e.holder: State Library of Modern and Contemporary History

12e1f5c3-c135-5c06-b2c9-4dc99c6e764e.third_name: *I gravi disordini a Cerignola (Foggia): la polizia disperde i contadini rivoltosi*
12e1f5c3-c135-5c06-b2c9-4dc99c6e764e.description2:
Agricultural workers were at the forefront of Italian labour movement. In 1901, they created the National Federation of Agricultural Workers (Federazione nazionale dei lavoratori della terra).  
In 1904, at Cerignola, the police violently repressed a protest of agricultural workers, killing 4 and injuring 40.

18b5dc74-b4d3-5829-af1b-731448b5f7c5.name: Sagesse College
18b5dc74-b4d3-5829-af1b-731448b5f7c5.description: The College's old building consists of a stone building with roof tiles and arcades, whereas the new building is a mostly concrete and glass structure. The College first opened its doors to students in 1874, although its construction was not fully completed until 1878 with the addition of a Church. The college's plan is horseshoe shaped facing the sea, and supposedly cost "about thirty thousand pieces of gold, including the purchase of surrounding land".
18b5dc74-b4d3-5829-af1b-731448b5f7c5.author: Hala Masri
18b5dc74-b4d3-5829-af1b-731448b5f7c5.history: Educational institutions in Lebanon were based on religion, as all the religious sects or confessions in Lebanon were in competition in the attempt to spread their beliefs and principles. The Maronite Christians struggled to build this institution due to the Ottoman presence. It was finally inaugurated by Archbishop Yussef Debs in 1875, and was heavily funded by France and Belgium. The construction of the building began in 1874 and lasted four years and cost approximately 30,000 pounds.

1961e839-9c16-5779-a767-870149fec738.name: The Serious Unemployment Crisis in the Province of Ferrara [central Italy]: Women Preventing the Cavalry from Advancing against the Rioters
1961e839-9c16-5779-a767-870149fec738.holder: State Library of Modern and Contemporary History

1961e839-9c16-5779-a767-870149fec738.third_name: *La grave crisi della disoccupazione in provincia di Ferrara: donne che impediscono alla cavalleria di avanzare contro i tumultuanti*
1961e839-9c16-5779-a767-870149fec738.second_name: Clashes between people who are protesting against unemployment and the army
1961e839-9c16-5779-a767-870149fec738.description2:
Violent clashes in the province of Ferrara (Emilia Romagna, Italy) between people who protested against unemployment and the army. The women are in the front line, protecting their comrades from the attacks of the cavalry.  
In 1913, an economic crisis hit Italy. Unemployment grew considerably and so did emigration. In 1913, Italian migration abroad reached its peak: 870.000 Italians migrate abroad. Social tensions and conflicts ran high.

1a906565-b92b-506c-8793-8e7de3c29e02.description2: The engraver Oscar Roty was famous for his image of "La Semeuse" (the sower), which was stamped on French coins.  This symbolic medallion, depicting two young students, pays tribute to Jules Ferry's education laws, which introduced free, secular and mandatory primary schooling for girls and boys.

2107c2f5-2fd6-5b2a-8227-d2730838e6b4.name: École Polytechnique du Bardo
2107c2f5-2fd6-5b2a-8227-d2730838e6b4.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
2107c2f5-2fd6-5b2a-8227-d2730838e6b4.history: Founded in 1837 and opened on the 5 March 1840 by order of the bey, the École Polytechnique du Bardo was the first military academy in Ottoman Tunisia. Conscious of Christian Europe's military superiority and following the example of the Ottoman Tanzimat reforms, Ahmed Pacha Bey set out to "modernise" the state and the army. The school was directed by an Italian Orientalist, the Colonel Luigi Calligaris with the help of a Tunisian scholar, Sheikh Mahmoud Kabadu. The state was forced to shut down the school in 1868 due to lack of funds. It educated the first generation of Tunisian who weren't hostile to the West.
2107c2f5-2fd6-5b2a-8227-d2730838e6b4.description2: Located inside the Palais du Bardo, this school offered a six year course to any 15 to 20 year old student who could pass its rigorous selection process. The best students would then go on to complete their studies at the École Saint-Cyr in France. The English, French and Italian professors here taught sciences as well as literature and French and Italian. The top students had their first real test when they were called to fight in the Crimean war of October 1854, and later in the resistance to the French occupation in 1881. Today, the school is located opposite the Musée du Bardo, and has preserved is grandiose façade decorated with Italian marble and the beylical coat of arms.

2183f178-ffa7-5b4a-bdf1-4af7eeca573c.name: Class photograph in Lehfed
2183f178-ffa7-5b4a-bdf1-4af7eeca573c.author: Hala Masri
2183f178-ffa7-5b4a-bdf1-4af7eeca573c.description2: This photograph was taken in Lehfed, a village in the Mount Lebanon district. The sign behind the children reads "*Vive L'Académie Imortelle Lehfed (Liban)*" (Long Live The Immortal Academy Lehfed (Lebanon)).

21ba2a39-e5d5-58c6-a42b-e97edf24cfc5.name: Gold medal awarded to l'École Emile-Loubet
21ba2a39-e5d5-58c6-a42b-e97edf24cfc5.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
21ba2a39-e5d5-58c6-a42b-e97edf24cfc5.description2: This certificate for a gold medal was awarded to the vocational college l'École Emile-Loubet in Tunis at the Paris International Trade Fair in 1900 for the training it provided particularly in carpentry, metalwork and book binding. The school was founded in 1898 by 'Ali Bey for teaching the basics of manual occupations. The bey, accompanied by the French President, placed the first stone of its new building in 1900, which then became the Lycée Technique Emile-Loubet.

23c0eaa7-284e-5a97-9ac8-8edafc208719.name: A petition to collect signatures in support of an appeal to the Italian parliament to grant women the right to vote, drawn up by Anna Maria Mozzoni
23c0eaa7-284e-5a97-9ac8-8edafc208719.holder: State Library of Modern and Contemporary History
23c0eaa7-284e-5a97-9ac8-8edafc208719.author: Rosanna De Longis
23c0eaa7-284e-5a97-9ac8-8edafc208719.description2:
With this appeal, Anna Maria Mozzoni and other women asked members of parliament to leave aside “academic digressions” on women’s nature and on their “mission” and to “consider we \[women\] only in our relation to the State, for what we really are: citizens, taxpayers, and able” who deserved the right to vote.  
Italian women’s campaign to get the right to vote gained momentum at the end of the 19th century and beginning of the 20th but it wasn’t successful until 1946.  
Anna Maria Mozzoni was the most brilliant Italian feminist activist of the second half of the 19th century. She authored books, founded journals and associations, and incessantly campaigned in favour of women’s rights.

24e0347f-f9f3-5254-ba16-aef618e16ba6.name: Flag
24e0347f-f9f3-5254-ba16-aef618e16ba6.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
24e0347f-f9f3-5254-ba16-aef618e16ba6.author: Huda Kilani
24e0347f-f9f3-5254-ba16-aef618e16ba6.description2: A piece of green Syrian silk fabric, inset on the top of the mast, which used to be carried during religious ceremonies. Trade and crafts were common activities in Jordan between the late 19th century and the earlier 20th century. These activities depended on migration and attracted groups of people who travelled or settled in the Jordanian territory to produce or sell products. Thus, the exchange of goods among different areas was very common, as exemplified by this object and many traditional dresses. Silk textiles were very common products in the Jordanian and Palestinian areas and were purchased from Syria, being an element in local fashion, both in Jordan and in Palestine.

2669ff94-bd70-55d1-a06b-cc0cbefd980d.name: The Great Mosque and University of Zaytuna
2669ff94-bd70-55d1-a06b-cc0cbefd980d.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
2669ff94-bd70-55d1-a06b-cc0cbefd980d.history: Located in the heart of the Tunis medina, the great Zaytuna Mosque is the largest and most revered religious site in Tunis. City life revolved around this mosque, as it was not only an important place of worship, but also a great university, with a reputation matching that of the Qaraouyine University in Fez and the al-Azhar University in Cairo. Many theologians and scholars of literature, arts and sciences were trained here for generations. Although it was the subject of many reforms in the 19th century, the modern Zaytuna University still provides a religious education, and attracts many believers at prayer times.
2669ff94-bd70-55d1-a06b-cc0cbefd980d.description2: An important place of worship, the Zaytuna mosque was subject to a great number of adjustments and expansions since its construction in the 7th century, most notably during the 17th and 18th centuries. The central courtyard is accessible through a suspended portico with horseshoe archways resting on beautiful columns topped with Hafsid capitals, through which the beautiful painted wooden ceilings can be seen. The paved courtyard is dominated by a square minaret, a beautiful sundial and a ribbed calotte which rests on an octagonal base above on a larger, square base. The décor is reminiscent of the Dome of the Rock in al-Quds (Jerusalem) in Palestine.

272951dc-4e51-55bc-bf53-6fb35a332aa6.name: Joint-stock company for iron, steel and railroad materials “Ferrotaie”. Factory for steel and railroad materials of Vado Ligure [Genoa, Italy]. Women working at milling machines

272951dc-4e51-55bc-bf53-6fb35a332aa6.archival: ACS, Ministero armi e munizioni, Ufficio storiografico della mobilitazione civile e industriale, Archivio fotografico, fasc. 112, foto 1516, neg. 3325B

272951dc-4e51-55bc-bf53-6fb35a332aa6.description2:
Women working in a steel and iron factory that produced materials of strategic value. The war had an important impact on women’s work. As historian Perry Willson pointed out, during WWI “women rarely directly substituted for men, instead tending to move into new work roles produced by wartime expansion.”  
In Italy, the number of women who worked in factories producing weapons and ammunitions rose from 23,000 in 1915 to 198,000 in 1918. Those numbers were far less than the women who participated in war production with more traditional “female roles”, such as making uniforms (400,000) or knitting woollen garments for the soldiers (200,000). However, Willson explained, women working in weapons’ factories had a relevance “as symbolic harbinger of change that greatly outweighed their actual numbers.”

27b52e92-40ef-53b5-9de2-ba320998fdf0.history: The Observatory was constructed with the support and sponsorship of King Pedro V (1837–1861). It began operating in 1867 and its first director was Frederico Oom, followed by Campos Rodrigues (1836–1919), an internationally recognised astronomer and a creator of several scientific instruments. In 1995, the Observatory integrated the University of Lisbon.
27b52e92-40ef-53b5-9de2-ba320998fdf0.keywords: Observatory; Scientific Heritage; Astronomy; National Museum of Natural History and Science; University of Lisbon
27b52e92-40ef-53b5-9de2-ba320998fdf0.architects: Architects: Jean François Gille Colson, José da Costa Sequeira (1800–1872), Valentim José Correia (1822–1900); Engineer: Frederico Augusto Oom (1830–1890)
27b52e92-40ef-53b5-9de2-ba320998fdf0.description2: The Lisbon Astronomical Observatory is the Portuguese national observatory. It has the legal responsibility of national timekeeping. It is located in the Tapada da Ajuda, a green area in the west of Lisbon. It is part of the Museums of the University of Lisbon/National Museum of Natural History and Science. It includes several buildings. It promotes activities regarding the public understanding of astronomy and astrophysics for diverse audiences. The Observatory has important collections: scientific instruments, mostly from the 19th and early 20th century; a Library, which is reference in Portugal, and an important historical archive.

28ec76df-2d4c-59e5-8b93-2cd4db3c1960.name: Labour certificate No.1(a) [Child’s labour certificate]
28ec76df-2d4c-59e5-8b93-2cd4db3c1960.author: Victoria and Albert Museum
28ec76df-2d4c-59e5-8b93-2cd4db3c1960.description2: Under the Employment of Children Act 1903, a child needed to obtain such a certificate (by passing a certain grade standard in school work) before being able to leave school and commence employment. The certificate is divided into two parallel sections, both stamped with the signature of James Graham, a Local Education Authority officer. The left-hand one gives the holder's name (Annie Waggonheim), address and birthdate, and certifies that she is not less than thirteen years old according to her birth certificate or statutory declaration. The right-hand section certifies that she has made 350 attendances in not more than two schools during each year for five preceding years, and gives 'Darley St C School' (Darley Street Council School) as the school in which the attendances were made.

2a226eef-1a17-51ae-9e21-911b78e227e7.name: The Builders
2a226eef-1a17-51ae-9e21-911b78e227e7.author: Marina Minozzi
2a226eef-1a17-51ae-9e21-911b78e227e7.keywords: Sculpture; Italian sculptors; reform; social change; work; post-unitarian Italian society; working class; working class condition; social topics; realism; Verismo; social verismo; artistic exchanges; France
2a226eef-1a17-51ae-9e21-911b78e227e7.copyright: Copyright image: Soprintendenza alla Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Moderna e Contemporanea.
2a226eef-1a17-51ae-9e21-911b78e227e7.description2: Arturo Dazzi was the son of the owner of a marble quarry and remained attracted to this raw material throughout his life. He attended the Academy of Fine Arts in Carrara and then won two national contests. The group of *The Builders*, as stated by the artist, was made for his final examination during the four years he spent at the Pensionato Nazionale di Scultura between 1904 to 1907. For this reason, the sculpture is very complicated and needed a lot of study and work in order to be completed. Nonetheless it gave great satisfaction to the artist: exhibited in 1907 in Italy and in 1909 in Munich the group was awarded both times with gold medals. The work shows an idealized version of the social “verism”, or truth, a concept common among young Italian sculptors of the time, and shows the influence of the painting of Constantin Meunier, *Enlèvement d’un creuset brisé*, done in 1884.

32533015-dfdb-5437-8c81-e020001b7470.description2:
‘The Suffragette’ was the weekly newspaper of the Woman's Social and Political Union (WSPU), the leading militant organisation campaigning for women’s suffrage in the United Kingdom. This wood block printed advertisement features the patron saint of the Suffragettes, Joan of Arc carrying the banner of the WSPU.  
  
Hilda Dallas was a member of the Suffrage Atelier, which was formed in 1909 to encourage artists to promote 'the enfranchisement of women, by means of pictorial publication'. Its activities also included training non-professional artists in printing techniques. The low cost, low tech method of wood block printing, as used in this poster, was cheap, quick and easy to learn.

355b8a63-ea50-5b91-9873-7e2c8152cab8.description2: Evangelism and colonialism often went hand in hand, working together to Christianise local populations. The missionaries considered French society as the perfect model of Christian society, and the government thought missions would help consolidate colonialism. Schools were one of the places where this relationship is the most evident. This image clearly shows how the French instilled young African children with love for the French flag from a very young age.

37bd3973-7cb4-5186-ac03-98cda4500caf.name: Ma’an honorary medal
37bd3973-7cb4-5186-ac03-98cda4500caf.description: A medal commemorating the victory of Arab armies over Ottoman forces in 1337/1918 and commemorating the leaders and the martyrs. On April 22nd, 1918 / AH Rajab 5th, 1337, Ma’an was captured by Arab forces after a decisive battle in which the Ottoman forces were defeated. King Hussein b. Ali created a medal bearing the name Ma’an medal, while the Arab revolts documents named it the Ma’an war memorial medal. On 11 August, 1919 when king Faisal became king of Syria, he issued a special law regarding the Ma’an medal, published in the official journal of the Faisal Government of Damascus, 13th November 1919; this law dictates seven articles. The medal formed two silver ears and two silver crossed swords surmounted by brass star. In other words, there is an equilateral triangle over each other and a ring on top. The two ears symbolize welfare and bestowal while the two swords are Arab Islamic Symbols of power and domination. In addition to that, the hexagonal star and Islamic Symbol appeared on Ayyubid and Mamluk Coins. The upper triangle tended upwards, the lower tended downwards, the word Ma’an is inscribed on the upper triangle in simple naskhi script and the date in A.H ١٣٣٧ is below. Historical novels indicate that the medal was made in France. The medal was given to 343 persons from the Arab World who were deemed worthy.

386fe084-5d31-5abb-9f36-fb457dd43935.name: Edward Jenner Inoculates his Small Son with the Smallpox Vaccine
386fe084-5d31-5abb-9f36-fb457dd43935.author: Marina Minozzi
386fe084-5d31-5abb-9f36-fb457dd43935.keywords: Medicine; health; vaccination; epidemics; disease; life expectancy; social changes; scientific development; social topics; post-unitarian Italian society; Positivism; celebration of science; international exhibitions; universal exposition

386fe084-5d31-5abb-9f36-fb457dd43935.third_name: *Edoardo Jenner inocula il vaccino del vaiolo al figlio*
386fe084-5d31-5abb-9f36-fb457dd43935.description2: Giulio Monteverde was an Italian sculptor who started carving wooden crucifixes before moving on to sculpture during his years at the Academy of Fine Arts in Genoa. In 1865 Monteverde moved to Rome to study at the Academy of St. Luke. The sculpture of Edward Jenner (1749-1823) represents the British physician and naturalist inoculating for the first time, on his own son, the smallpox vaccine that he invented. This work was initially rejected by the Academy of St. Luke, entrusted with selecting works of art for the International Exposition in Vienna, but then exhibited in it thanks to an influential friend. The plaster cast of Jenner won the gold medal in Vienna, and a similar success was had with the marble version presented at the Universal Exhibition in Paris in 1878 when it won the medal of honor. The bronze version shown in the picture represents Jenner administering the smallpox vaccine to his son, blending dynamism and details in the face of the scientist, clothes and objects.

3a9203b3-ee28-58a5-9738-28760f62fc9b.name: Photograph
3a9203b3-ee28-58a5-9738-28760f62fc9b.dimensions: Height: 27.5 cm album, Width: 80 cm album open
3a9203b3-ee28-58a5-9738-28760f62fc9b.author: Victoria and Albert Museum
3a9203b3-ee28-58a5-9738-28760f62fc9b.description2:
This photograph is taken from a family photograph album. Most of the photographs in it are printed on platinum paper, which was introduced in 1879.  
Throughout most of the 19th century women had few legal rights to property, money, children, or even, after marriage, their own bodies. However, there were great changes in attitudes during the last decade of the century. The traditional role of women was questioned and some women openly defied convention. They educated themselves by reading widely and took up what were seen as 'un-ladylike' activities such as smoking and cycling. The free movement of the bicycle was seen as a symbol of equality and personal freedom.

3adb9096-0d5a-502e-a3c7-2ce892e11f6a.name: Beirut Evangelical School for Girls and Boys
3adb9096-0d5a-502e-a3c7-2ce892e11f6a.description: Beirut Evangelical School is located in Rabiye, a wealthy area in Metn, Mount Lebanon. The school covers all levels from nursery, to elementary, intermediate and secondary schooling. It consists of two large buildings that house all the school's classes, laboratories, offices and administration, as well as a church and the administrative Synod Building of Syria and Lebanon. The facades are covered in a yellow and blue coating.
3adb9096-0d5a-502e-a3c7-2ce892e11f6a.author: Hady El Hajj, Jennifer Harb, Cynthia Karaki
3adb9096-0d5a-502e-a3c7-2ce892e11f6a.history: The Beirut Evangelical School for Girls and Boys is one of the oldest educational institutions in Lebanon, first founded in 1835. It has its roots in the first school for girls founded in west Beirut in 1828 by the early American Presbyterian missionaries to Greater Syria. In 1959, the Presbyterian Church in the USA transferred to the National Evangelical Synod of Syria and Lebanon and who henceforth were responsible for the running of all the educational institutions in the area that had been founded by American Presbyterian missionaries.

3cd68daa-dde5-568b-8623-dcdb17c2cf59.name: One piaster/Type 2

Marginal legend: “*amara bi-ta‘amul ‘abduhu wa-ibn ‘abdihi / sana 8*” (“It is orders to deal with, God’s Servant and son of God’s Servant, Year 8”). 3d283460-a96d-52c9-8396-14cc20cc6366.name: A young algerian girl
3d283460-a96d-52c9-8396-14cc20cc6366.description2: Between the late 19th century and the 1930s, it became fashionable in the West to take photographs of children, either for publication as postcards or with "anthropological" aims. This photograph highlights the striking contrast between the hardships of poverty and the young girl's smile.

3f2975b9-cd05-5386-b04d-d6926ecba53e.name: Women in the Revolution of 1919
3f2975b9-cd05-5386-b04d-d6926ecba53e.keywords: 1919 Revolution; Egyptian Revolutions; Egyptian Women; Political Participation
3f2975b9-cd05-5386-b04d-d6926ecba53e.description2: The Egyptian women of the 1919 Revolution – one of the most important Egyptian revolutions in modern times – which started due to objections to the practices of British occupation and the exile of symbols of Egyptian patriotism.

427b0484-9935-51b8-bf73-9f3ed319e742.name: Laboratorio Chimico of Lisbon Polytechnic School
427b0484-9935-51b8-bf73-9f3ed319e742.holder: National Museum of Natural History and Science (MUHNAC) / Museums of the University of Lisbon
427b0484-9935-51b8-bf73-9f3ed319e742.author: Marta C. Lourenço (MUHNAC-UL)
427b0484-9935-51b8-bf73-9f3ed319e742.history: The Laboratorio Chimico was built in the 1850s, later profoundly restructured during the 1880s and 90s. It was intensely used for teaching and research until 1998, when the Chemistry Department moved to the new campus of the Faculty of Sciences at cidade universitária. The complementary laboratories and rooms were quite modified during the 1960s and 1970s due to the large increase of teachers, students and researchers. The Museum started its recovery and musealization in 1998, which sought restitution of the original design of the Laboratorio’s golden age (1890s) in all areas. Therefore the 60s and 70s partitions and mezzanines were removed. The Laboratorio opened to the public in 2007.
427b0484-9935-51b8-bf73-9f3ed319e742.keywords: Chemistry; History of Chemistry; Laboratory; Integrated Heritage; National Museum of Natural History and Science; University of Lisbon
427b0484-9935-51b8-bf73-9f3ed319e742.architects: Author of the Laboratorio Chimico, gallery and amphitheatre: architect João Pedro Monteiro (original project dating from 1852, continued by Pierre-Joseph Pézerat); A considerable refurbishment was supervised by José Júlio Bettencourt Rodrigues between 1888 and 1890 but the architect is unknown
427b0484-9935-51b8-bf73-9f3ed319e742.description2: The Laboratorio, together with the Amphitheatre and other complementary areas, occupies a surface area of 800 m2 in the west wing of the main building of MUHNAC. Its monumentality, functionality have been praised since its construction. In a first approach it has relevance for its beauty, singularity and for the authentic atmosphere provided to visitors. The Laboratorio Chimico is relevant for the history of chemistry and its teaching, particularly in Portugal, and it’s a historical document in itself, completed by a vast archival and iconographic documentation that complements and enhances the Laboratorio’s importance as a source for the history of science. Finally, the existence of one of the most important chemistry collections of Europe, derived from this site, is worth mentioning.

433df55d-0327-5977-a447-ca5420a7ce29.name: Laënnec examining a patient at the Necker Hospital in 1816
433df55d-0327-5977-a447-ca5420a7ce29.description2: The 19th century saw a number of important advances in the medical field. René Laënnec (1781–1926) was a French doctor who invented the stethoscope, allowing him to improve medical diagnoses by listening to patients' chests. Doctors were thus able to analyse sounds inside the body, and link them to illnesses such as tuberculosis, which was very common in the 19th century.

43887649-28e4-5e71-ad7d-9a1cc8750dfc.name: *Art exhibition at school, 12–25 June, 1904*
43887649-28e4-5e71-ad7d-9a1cc8750dfc.description2: The introduction of art as a primary school subject was a long and difficult process. Linear drawing was introduced first with a utilitarian objective. From 1879, teaching art became mandatory due to a standardization of teaching practices, and specialised teachers were recruited for this purpose. From the early 20th century onwards art became, supposedly, the art of depicting reality. Various organisations also pushed for the democratisation of art in schools. This poster shows a school student taking interest in famous paintings, such as those by Millet.

43a8c5d9-b3aa-529b-a3f9-5e64b5b32a48.name: The Pearl Carpet
43a8c5d9-b3aa-529b-a3f9-5e64b5b32a48.materials: Pearls, silk, deer hide, beads, gems
43a8c5d9-b3aa-529b-a3f9-5e64b5b32a48.description2: The foundation of silk and fine deer hide is densely embroidered overall with a design worked in strings of natural ‘Basra’ pearls, measuring approximately 1-3 mm, and English coloured glass beads. There are on average 78 pearls and beads per vertical dm. (10 cm), and 68 per horizontal dm., equaling a density of c.4,990 pearls and beads per dm2. The total area of the carpet is c. 45,670 cm2. The 32 smaller rosettes cover an area of c. 400 cm2 with smaller gems, and the total area embroidered with pearls and is beads is approximately 44,500 cm2. Therefore, over 2.2 million pearls and beads have been used to decorate the field. In our estimation, the number of pearls employed in the design is therefor at least 1.2-1.5 million.

443b06f0-b14c-5ef9-9ab2-20b5d7d56003.name: *Clothes for prisoners of war. Charitable organisation attached the French \[Red Cross\]. Donations both in cash and in kind should be delivered to the organisation's headquarters, at 63 Avenue des Champs-Elysées.*
443b06f0-b14c-5ef9-9ab2-20b5d7d56003.keywords: Hygiene; Red Cross; First World War
443b06f0-b14c-5ef9-9ab2-20b5d7d56003.description2: Throughout the First World War, many charitable organisations came to the aid of soldiers and civilian populations in occupied territories. They carried out poster campaigns or published appeals in the press to obtain donations. This poster depicts a military prisoner of war's sadness as he writes to his loved ones. The Red Cross supervised these charitable partnerships in order to ensure the safe arrival of the donations in "enemy" territory.

453156d3-f141-581a-96a5-4ef8c83cbae1.name: Dr Charles Nicolle
453156d3-f141-581a-96a5-4ef8c83cbae1.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
453156d3-f141-581a-96a5-4ef8c83cbae1.description2: Pictured here is Dr. Charles Nicolle, a French microbiology doctor born in Rouen on 21 September 1966, in his research laboratory. His name is strongly linked to l'Institut Pasteur, which he directed from 1903–1936, playing the role of administrator, researcher, school headmaster, and advocate for the teaching of hygiene and illness prevention. In 1928 he received the Nobel Prize for Physiology. He died in 1936 and is buried at the Institut Pasteur, where his tombstone is engraved with olive and apple tree branches crossed over, the symbols of Tunisia and Normandy.

4590fdc2-d3b9-5462-8feb-df1ae40b4e9e.name: *Lesson at the Benaki Orphanage in Alexandria Egypt*
4590fdc2-d3b9-5462-8feb-df1ae40b4e9e.author: Maria Dimitriadou
4590fdc2-d3b9-5462-8feb-df1ae40b4e9e.description2: Geometry lesson in Benakio Orphanage in Alexandria. Photographer Asiz e Dores.

462d8120-9ece-5f2c-b1f7-e362d936bd2d.name: L'École de la Rue du Pacha (classrooom exit)
462d8120-9ece-5f2c-b1f7-e362d936bd2d.holder: Institut Supérieur d’Histoire Contemporaine de la Tunisie
462d8120-9ece-5f2c-b1f7-e362d936bd2d.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
462d8120-9ece-5f2c-b1f7-e362d936bd2d.description2: The school founded by Louise-Renée-Millet, opened 1 May 1900, was the first public school for young Muslim girls. Pictured here are the young girls as they enter school, veiled, accompanied and under the strict gaze of their French teachers. Subsidised by the French Resident-General until it was taken over by a *habous*, the school came under the government's jurisdiction between 1911 and 1912, and was then moved to a new residence on the Rue du Pacha. Despite its humble beginnings, with just five students, the school steadily expanded. Nabeul, Sousse, and Kairouan, on the inside of the country, soon followed suit and opened their own public schools. L'École de la Rue du Pacha held the held the important position as the first school of its kind, as well as the cradle for many important members of the first generation of political militants and feminist activists.

464aad1f-7be1-5c39-ab67-b2b1cb16454a.name: General meeting on women's suffrage
464aad1f-7be1-5c39-ab67-b2b1cb16454a.description2: Throughout the 19th and early 20th centuries, a number of different political movements for votes for women emerged, all using many different tactics. For example in May 1908, following the English model, a group of "suffragettes" held a protest during the Paris municipal elections, in which their actions (upturning ballot boxes, breaking polling station windows) were controversial. The following month, a national congress on women's rights and suffrage was held in Paris, an act which was hugely symbolic in and of itself. Their struggle was a long one, and it was not until 1944 that French women obtained the right to vote, which they exercised for the first time in 1945.

4884a720-8e5b-52db-b680-609daaf48e72.name: Flag of the Italian Socialist Party’s local branch in a small village near Turin (Cafasse Torinese), bearing the image of a worker breaking a sword (an icon of antimilitarism)
4884a720-8e5b-52db-b680-609daaf48e72.author: Giulia Barrera
4884a720-8e5b-52db-b680-609daaf48e72.archival: ACS, Partito nazionale fascista, Mostra della Rivoluzione fascista
4884a720-8e5b-52db-b680-609daaf48e72.description2:
The Italian Socialist Party opposed Italian participation in World War I. After the government and the King decided to enter the war on the side of French and Britain, the Socialist’s Party line became “né aderire, né sabotare” (neither support, nor sabotage). Anti-war sentiments remained widespread among workers and peasants. In August 1917, without any prior organisation by the Socialist Party or by the trade union, spontaneous bread riots erupted in Turin: women led marchers that demanded bread and the end of the war, and they looted shops and barracks. Such protests were harshly repressed.  
War casualties were very high: 650,000 military deaths, 950,000 wounded, 600.000 prisoners of war or missing.

4974cb0e-719c-5e1f-975e-0b6646dd1058.name: Notarial seal from Amman
4974cb0e-719c-5e1f-975e-0b6646dd1058.keywords: Seal; city; Jordan; urban model; tribe; settler; Ottoman
4974cb0e-719c-5e1f-975e-0b6646dd1058.description2: Seal made of a round brass disc, inscribed clockwise in *divan* script: “*Amman Nahyan sand Achrafieh mahallasi mukhtar awwal 330*". In the middle there is a round hollow to hold a second seal, bearing the title *mukhtar*, illustrating the fact that, in order to stamp official papers, two seals were needed: one belonging to the quarter, the other belonging to the *mukhtar*. The seal has a pierced handle in the back and a new chain to hold it and to keep it with the *mukhtar*. Amman was a small district (*Nahyan*) in the Ottoman administrative division, following al-Salt province (*qada’*). The *Nahyan* was divided administratively into quarters or tribal units, each one called *mahalla*. Each mahalla had a mayor (*mukhtar*) who was responsible for the verification of births, deaths, marriage affairs, bachelorhood and land affairs. The mukhtar was elected from tribal notables of the quarters. The seal belonged to the first mukhtar of the Achrafieh quarter, “Achrafieh Mahallasi”, in Amman AH 1330 / AD 1911. Achrafieh quarter, as indicated in court records of Amman, existed before the year AH 1338 / AD 1919. It seems that this quarter was the extension of Qabertai quarter which was located below the west south of Amman Citadel, opposite to al-‘Umari mosque. A bridge called the Roman bridge connected the two quarters.

4a9e8faf-67a9-5069-bc5f-ea7ea5a901a7.name: The hair cut
4a9e8faf-67a9-5069-bc5f-ea7ea5a901a7.author: Hala Masri
4a9e8faf-67a9-5069-bc5f-ea7ea5a901a7.description2: Portrait of a boarding school student.

4afba372-f646-5f65-bf2a-c007b03e354e.name: Secondary school students giving a sports performance during King Fu`ad I's visit to the Fayum Directorate
4afba372-f646-5f65-bf2a-c007b03e354e.description2: A sports show by secondary school students at the Directorate of Fayum, presented before King Fu`ad I. The importance of the picture comes down to its rarity, especially its reference to the field visit conducted by King Fu`ad I.

4be86fc9-7fe9-524a-8ea0-665de458829d.name: The Italian woman poet and peace activist of Armenian descent Vittoria Aganoor Pompilj (1855–1910), and a signed copy of her poem 'Peace'
4be86fc9-7fe9-524a-8ea0-665de458829d.type: Photograph and autograph collected in a register
4be86fc9-7fe9-524a-8ea0-665de458829d.author: Maria Grazia Bistoni, Costanza Maria Del Giudice
4be86fc9-7fe9-524a-8ea0-665de458829d.archival: AS PG, Società per la pace e l'arbitrato internazionale di Perugia, 10
4be86fc9-7fe9-524a-8ea0-665de458829d.description2: The descendant of an Armenian family that migrated to Venice at the beginning of the 19th century, Vittoria Aganoor Pompilj authored poems that were translated during her life into English, French and Spanish. She corresponded with many international literary figures and was a member of the International Arbitration and Peace League of Perugia (*Società per la pace e l'arbitrato internazionale di Perugia*), founded in 1892. In 1870, the British trade unionist Randal Cremer (Nobel peace laureate in 1907) founded the International Arbitration League, which –among other things – protested British intervention in Egypt and imperialism.

4c22f475-8576-51f3-bde0-fc0eadf0e0ec.name: Italian Company Westinghouse. Factory at Vado Ligure [Genoa, Italy]. The Production of Ogives for Shells
4c22f475-8576-51f3-bde0-fc0eadf0e0ec.author: Cristina Mosillo, Giulia Barrera
4c22f475-8576-51f3-bde0-fc0eadf0e0ec.archival: ACS, Ministero armi e munizioni, Ufficio storiografico della mobilitazione civile e industriale, Archivio fotografico, fasc. 156, foto 2134, neg. 379 B.
4c22f475-8576-51f3-bde0-fc0eadf0e0ec.third_name: Soc. Italiana Westinghouse. Stabilimento di Vado ligure (GE). Lavorazione per ogive per proiettili
4c22f475-8576-51f3-bde0-fc0eadf0e0ec.second_name: Women working in a factory that produced military equipment, during World War I
4c22f475-8576-51f3-bde0-fc0eadf0e0ec.description2:
Women working in an Italian factory that produced military equipment, during WWI. The war had an important impact on women’s work. As historian Perry Willson pointed out, during WWI “women rarely directly substituted for men, instead tending to move into new work roles produced by wartime expansion.”  
In Italy, the number of women who worked in factory producing weapons and ammunitions rose from 23,000 in 1915 to 198,000 in 1918. The numbers were far less than the women who participated in war production with more traditional “female roles”, such as making uniforms (400,000) or knitting woolen garments for the soldiers (200,000). However, Willson explained, women working in weapons’ factories had a relevance “as symbolic harbinger of change that greatly outweighed their actual numbers.”

en: Willson, Perry R., *Women in Twentieth-century Italy*, New York: Palgrave Macmillan, 2010.

4c5ec9e7-571c-57c0-a345-64717d007c10.name: *Nazareth School*
4c5ec9e7-571c-57c0-a345-64717d007c10.author: Hady El Hajj, Jennifer Harb, Cynthia Karaki
4c5ec9e7-571c-57c0-a345-64717d007c10.description2: Pictured here is the Nazareth School, founded in 1868 by Mother Pauline de Vaux, Superior General of the Congregation of the Ladies of Nazareth. The decision to found this school was supported by the Bishop Vallegra, in Rome. It was first located in a large house in the European quarter of Beirut, nicknamed "The Blue Castle". However, with the number of students rapidly growing, the school had to relocate. In 1877 the new convent was opened for this purpose on St. George Hill, bought by the *firman* of Constantinople. The building is U-shaped and made of stone, with white cloisters and surrounded by a huge garden.

4c5f8ec8-becc-59f0-937c-3cc5e1969665.name: The digging of the Western Canal of the Aswan Dam
4c5f8ec8-becc-59f0-937c-3cc5e1969665.description2:
Hundreds of Egyptian labourers digging the western canal of the Aswan Dam.  
Located in Upper Egypt, the Aswan Dam was the first water storage project in modern times.

4d5b7131-33fe-5c5d-8076-ab9568f98e94.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
4d5b7131-33fe-5c5d-8076-ab9568f98e94.author: Huda Kilani
4d5b7131-33fe-5c5d-8076-ab9568f98e94.keywords: coffee; coffee roasting; coffee beans; domestic furnishing
4d5b7131-33fe-5c5d-8076-ab9568f98e94.description2: Circular iron coffee roaster with long handle decorated with zigzag and triangle motifs. Coffee-drinking in a communal setting is an essential part of traditions in Bedouin communities to celebrate or mourn.

50ff7499-1e83-52e9-88c7-d80dd581fe29.name: Photograph "Under the Oak Tree"
50ff7499-1e83-52e9-88c7-d80dd581fe29.description: Pictured here is the priest Joseph Delore, speaking to a group of children. Boys are seated at the front, whereas girls, whose hair is covered by a white scarf, are seated at the back.

51101afe-20b5-5b27-9fe9-38dbf49761d6.name: The Imam Uza'i Mosque
51101afe-20b5-5b27-9fe9-38dbf49761d6.author: Hala Masri
51101afe-20b5-5b27-9fe9-38dbf49761d6.history: The name of Imam Uza'i, who died twelve centuries ago, is often associated with the values of tolerance, justice, and brotherhood. Born in Baalbek in the year 681, 'Abd al-Rahman Uza'i was a strong advocate of justice, freedom and mercy over what he considered to be the religious fanaticism and human autocracy of his time. He stood alongside Lebanese Christians in his fervent opposition to the Abbasid regime. He was also a renowned thinker and intellectual. After relocating to Beirut he soon begun to accept visitors in his home where he offered advice and imparted wisdom. To this day, thousands of Lebanese visit his mausoleum in search for blessings and mercy.
51101afe-20b5-5b27-9fe9-38dbf49761d6.description2: The Imam Uza'i Mosque, with its green dome and two minarets, contains the tomb of Imam Uza'i, who died in 774. It became a religious school in the 19th century which is still in use today.

52254363-31d0-54f5-bab4-97458eb40b9d.name: Vanadinite
52254363-31d0-54f5-bab4-97458eb40b9d.holder: National Museum of Natural History and Science (MUHNAC) / Museums of the University of Lisbon
52254363-31d0-54f5-bab4-97458eb40b9d.author: Liliana Póvoas (MUHNAC-UL)
52254363-31d0-54f5-bab4-97458eb40b9d.keywords: Vanadinite crystals; Apatite group; hexagonal system; vanadium ore; National Museum of Natural History and Science; University of Lisbon
52254363-31d0-54f5-bab4-97458eb40b9d.description2: Vanadinite crystals on matrix. Vanadinite is a vanadate mineral with the chemical formula Pb5(VO4)3Cl. This mineral species was named Vanadinite (1839) because it contains vanadium. It belongs to the Apatite group of phosphates. Crystals of vanadinite conform to the hexagonal system of symmetry. These Vanadinite crystals are short prismatic, with smooth faces and sharp hedges. Their colour is orange-red and they are nearly opaque. And they present an intense resinous lustre. Vanadinite occurs as a secondary mineral in the oxidized zone of lead-bearing deposits and it is one of the main industrial ores of the element vanadium. This sample has been collected at Mibladen Mine, Midelt, Khénifra Province, Morocco.
52254363-31d0-54f5-bab4-97458eb40b9d.holding_institution_org: Museu Nacional da Historia Natural e da Ciencia (MUHNAC)

52bc1f5c-19f1-5c15-8794-630ecd367289.name: Amulet
52bc1f5c-19f1-5c15-8794-630ecd367289.type: Cultic Object; ornament; talismanic object; jewellery
52bc1f5c-19f1-5c15-8794-630ecd367289.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
52bc1f5c-19f1-5c15-8794-630ecd367289.author: Huda Kilani
52bc1f5c-19f1-5c15-8794-630ecd367289.keywords: Talisman; crescent; tusks; wild boar; heal of Gazalle
52bc1f5c-19f1-5c15-8794-630ecd367289.description2: This object is a piece of horse jewellery, an amulet worn around the horse's neck to ward off misfortune. Horse jewellery was used among Bedouins and villagers communities. This amulet consists of a silver-cased crescent composed of two joined tusks of wild boar. A ¼ Majidi Ottoman gold coin dangles from the crescent with three crescents and stars at the end. The silver chain is called “heal of gazelle”.

5417f6b5-cc8c-53f1-96de-52e25282f580.name: An Egyptian woman giving a public speech during the events of the 1919 Revolution
5417f6b5-cc8c-53f1-96de-52e25282f580.keywords: 1919 Revolution; Egyptian Revolutions; Egyptian Women; Political Participation
5417f6b5-cc8c-53f1-96de-52e25282f580.description2: An Egyptian woman talking to the crowds, encouraging them to fight for their rights. The 1919 Revolution – one of the most important Egyptian revolutions in modern times– started due to objections to the practices of the British occupation and the exile of symbols of Egyptian patriotism.

541b2d25-7056-5660-8154-f73cfaa855f5.name: Qasr al-`Ayni Hospital Administrative Employees
541b2d25-7056-5660-8154-f73cfaa855f5.keywords: Medicine; Doctors; Qasr al-`Ayni Hospital; Egyptian Hospitals; Administrators
541b2d25-7056-5660-8154-f73cfaa855f5.description2: Photograph of the administrative employees at Qasr al-`Ayni Hospital.

54310c6d-87ca-585e-b552-bcb1c5951fe3.name: Dress
54310c6d-87ca-585e-b552-bcb1c5951fe3.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
54310c6d-87ca-585e-b552-bcb1c5951fe3.author: Huda Kilani
54310c6d-87ca-585e-b552-bcb1c5951fe3.materials: Silk, cotton; hand woven Syrian silk fabric (brocade)
54310c6d-87ca-585e-b552-bcb1c5951fe3.description2: This dress of al-Druze (Druse) women is made of a long grey with green and silver brocade, pursed narrow sleeves, wide, open square shaped chest, pursed at the middle and wide at the bottom with ruffles and a cotton liner. This object illustrates the variegated social composition and demographic changes in the Jordanian territory in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The al-Druze tribes migrated from Syria (Hawran) to north east Jordan in the early twentieth century because of their support for the Syrian revolution against the French occupation. The traditional Druse and other Jordanian costumes were influenced by the local trade and economic activities: as illustrated in this case, they were often made of silk textiles, produced in Syria and traded to Jordan and Palestine.

54a75fca-9a38-5dc2-9f8e-80faf09f8470.name: *The Artist Girl and Her Studio*
54a75fca-9a38-5dc2-9f8e-80faf09f8470.keywords: Painting; Halil Pasha; orientalist Turkish painters
54a75fca-9a38-5dc2-9f8e-80faf09f8470.description2: The basis of Turkish painting drawing influence from western tradition was laid when *Mühendishane-i Berr-i Hümayun* (the Naval Academy) opened in 1795. Halil Pasha, who had been a student of the painting courses held at the Academy, was foremost among the painters with a military background who founded a western style art tradition in Turkey. He worked with Jean Leon Gerome in his atelier in Paris. He provided a unique distinction to the analysis of impressionist light and colour, and was an example of artists dealing with impressionist technique. Because of his qualified knowledge about anatomy and his interest in depicting the human figure, Halil Pasha had a unique place in Turkish Art History.

58837723-b1a0-5787-a2b8-812f79e409c5.name: Dr Charles Nicolle, Nobel Laureate for Medicine
58837723-b1a0-5787-a2b8-812f79e409c5.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
58837723-b1a0-5787-a2b8-812f79e409c5.description2: This is a photograph of Dr Charles Nicolle carrying out child vaccination on the indigenous Tunisian population. During his time at l'Institut Pasteur (1903–1936) he worked to prevent or eradicate infectious illnesses

5984df39-df0b-5179-8186-0d620e962e8c.name: Portrait of Butrus al-Bustani
5984df39-df0b-5179-8186-0d620e962e8c.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Hassan El Masri, Remy Nader
5984df39-df0b-5179-8186-0d620e962e8c.description2: Butrus al-Bustani was born in Debbeye, and studied at Ayn Warka School for ten years. He was appointed professor at this school at the age of 20, before moving to teach in the American College of 'Abeyh. He then moved to Beirut, where he became an interpreter at the US consulate, working with American missionaries and their printing press. He published numerous important books, including his famous Encyclopedia, and founded the National School of Beirut. He died in May 1883.

59e91077-81f0-5cb2-9fc1-2e7eb98c95ab.name: Turkish woman
59e91077-81f0-5cb2-9fc1-2e7eb98c95ab.description2: The Zangaki brothers were a pair of photographers working in Egypt who sold "Orientalist" photos to Western tourists. This photograph for example, responds to Western stereotypes by depicting a Turkish woman lying nonchalantly by shisha pipe.

5a482712-4636-5e5b-aa8a-6973d1c66d25.name: *The Approach to Nablus (Shechem)*
5a482712-4636-5e5b-aa8a-6973d1c66d25.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
5a482712-4636-5e5b-aa8a-6973d1c66d25.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
5a482712-4636-5e5b-aa8a-6973d1c66d25.artist: Josiah Wood Whymper (after a pencil drawing by Harry Fenn 1838–1911)
5a482712-4636-5e5b-aa8a-6973d1c66d25.description2: This image shows the approach to Nablus (at the time believed to mark the biblical Shechem, according to the Bible first capital of the Kingdom of Israel and situated in the vicinity of several important Abrahamic sites). The caption further explains that the view is taken through the olive groves on the eastern side of the city, and that 'the gate is shown beneath the minaret'. The artist who created this work, Josiah Wood Whymper, was a British watercolour painter, engraver, and illustrator, who apparently never left Britain, but provided a prolific body of engravings to publishers, in particular the Society for the Promotion of Christian Knowledge. This print originally appeared in Vol. 1, page 243 of Charles William Wilson's  'Pituresque Palestine, Sinai and Egypt', published between 1881 and 1884.

5bdb7155-07a2-5eb8-97fb-cb481391296f.name: A photo of the Dairy Laboratory at Fu`ad Agricultural Museum
5bdb7155-07a2-5eb8-97fb-cb481391296f.dates: 16 January 1938 (Photo taken during the inauguration of the museum)
5bdb7155-07a2-5eb8-97fb-cb481391296f.description2: The Fu`ad Agriculture Museum was considered the first of its kind in the Middle East and the Arab World during the 1930s. It was inaugurated during the time of King Faruq, the son of King Fu`ad, and houses a large number of collections related to agricultural and rural environments, as well as agricultural plants and animals.

5c7df1fd-3c74-5952-b9c6-f24375461c19.name: *The Egyptian University – Faculty of Medicine*
5c7df1fd-3c74-5952-b9c6-f24375461c19.keywords: Education; Students; Faculty of Medicine; Egyptian University
5c7df1fd-3c74-5952-b9c6-f24375461c19.description2:
General view of the Egyptian University Faculty of Medicine and Qasr al-\`Ayni Hospital in 1933.  
The 1923 Constitution stipulated that “Primary education is mandatory for all Egyptian boys and girls”. A decree was issued for the establishment of a public university under the name “The Egyptian University” in 1925, comprised of four faculties; literature, science, medicine and law. The Faculty of Medicine, annexed to Qasr al-\`Ayni Hospital, is one of the leading hospitals in the Arab World.

5ca32455-94fe-56af-a57b-31d8cd317caf.name: Flag possibly belonging to a group of miners with anarchist ideas, bearing the sign “Neither servants nor masters, nor a penny nor a soldier”
5ca32455-94fe-56af-a57b-31d8cd317caf.author: Giulia Barrera
5ca32455-94fe-56af-a57b-31d8cd317caf.archival: ACS, Partito nazionale fascista, Mostra della Rivoluzione fascista
5ca32455-94fe-56af-a57b-31d8cd317caf.third_name: *Né servi né padroni, né un soldo né un soldato*
5ca32455-94fe-56af-a57b-31d8cd317caf.description2: Flag possibly belonging to a group of miners with anarchist leanings (anarchists used black flags, and the working tools represented on the flag were used by miners), bearing on one side the sign: “neither servants nor masters”, and on the other side, the sign “Nor a penny nor a soldier” (it was implied “for the war”) and the image of broken weapons.

en: Centro studi Piero Gobetti, *Un' altra Italia nelle bandiere dei lavoratori: simboli e cultura dall'unità d'Italia all'avvento del fascismo*, Turin: Centro studi Piero Gobetti, 1980.

5d84c4b0-6f1a-5b1c-87d0-3d8a61317a0a.name: Flag of the Female Workers Friendly Society (Società di mutuo soccorso femminile) of Cremona, bearing the motto “All for one and one for all”
5d84c4b0-6f1a-5b1c-87d0-3d8a61317a0a.dates: Unknown (probably end of the 19th–beginning of the 20th century)
5d84c4b0-6f1a-5b1c-87d0-3d8a61317a0a.author: Angela Bellardi
5d84c4b0-6f1a-5b1c-87d0-3d8a61317a0a.archival: ASCr, Società di mutuo soccorso femminile di Cremona
5d84c4b0-6f1a-5b1c-87d0-3d8a61317a0a.description2:
During the second half of the 19th century, “friendly societies” flourished in Italy (especially in Central and Northern Italy). They predated trade unionism and were an important element of Italian social life.  
The Female Friendly Society (Società di mutuo soccorso femminile) of Cremona was created in 1863. It mostly comprised factory workers such as spinners and other workers in textile industry, but also included craftswomen like self-employed dressmakers, and even a few teachers.

5dff6363-db06-5f8b-a5b7-182ee09e3ba6.name: Gas burner
5dff6363-db06-5f8b-a5b7-182ee09e3ba6.holder: National Museum of Natural History and Science (MUHNAC) / Museums of the University of Lisbon
5dff6363-db06-5f8b-a5b7-182ee09e3ba6.author: Marta C. Lourenço (MUHNAC-UL)
5dff6363-db06-5f8b-a5b7-182ee09e3ba6.artist: Maker unknown, the object is unsigned

5dff6363-db06-5f8b-a5b7-182ee09e3ba6.description2: The object is a set of four Bunsen burners, in metal. Each burner has its own regulation valve for gas. The Bunsen Burner is still today widely used in chemistry laboratories.

60b297ce-03b5-5b81-8b64-abe6de2613c4.name: The Various Ages of Woman
60b297ce-03b5-5b81-8b64-abe6de2613c4.holder: Central Institute for Ethno-Anthropology, National Museum of Arts and Popular Traditions
60b297ce-03b5-5b81-8b64-abe6de2613c4.author: Marina Minozzi
60b297ce-03b5-5b81-8b64-abe6de2613c4.keywords: Popular traditions; ethnology; anthropology; post-unitarian Italian society; work; agriculture; pastoralism; ethnographic exhibition; exhibition; collection; collector; museum; woman; migration; internal migration; city; countriside; rural space
60b297ce-03b5-5b81-8b64-abe6de2613c4.copyright: Copyright image: Roma, Istituto Centrale per la Demoetnoantropologia, ICDE, Archivio storico.
60b297ce-03b5-5b81-8b64-abe6de2613c4.description2: The National Museum of Popular Arts and Traditions in Rome was founded by Lamberto Loria (1855–1913), an Italian ethnologist passionate about the need to record the agro-pastoral Italian culture that was disappearing to industrialization and the consequent migration from the countryside towards the cities. In 1911, 50th anniversary of Italian unification, or Risorgimento, Loria organized the Italian Ethnographic Exhibition in Rome. Through the help of a group of coworkers, Loria gathered over three-thousand objects from exhibition of 1911, which today form the principal nucleus of the Museum’s collections.

61817120-0f01-5c48-bcf7-a52ed14728f7.name: School of North African girls directed by Mme Luce. Studying.
61817120-0f01-5c48-bcf7-a52ed14728f7.second_name: Taken from *L'Algerie Phtographiée*, vol. 2, Province d'Alger
61817120-0f01-5c48-bcf7-a52ed14728f7.description2: French colonisation of Algeria deprived the Algerian schooling system of its traditional funding and brought it into disorder, as very few "indigenous Muslim" students were accepted into the new European schools. A few private initiatives emerged, such as this establishment for young Muslim women, founded by Madame Luce Allix in 1846.

63e28bd3-5d45-5462-b773-fca1e9fbcffb.name: Photograph illustrating the response to the government's public vaccination campaign

6918edf0-4e2e-58b2-82d5-437119b828fa.name: Lycée Armand-Fallières
6918edf0-4e2e-58b2-82d5-437119b828fa.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
6918edf0-4e2e-58b2-82d5-437119b828fa.keywords: Colonial school; Franco-Arab school; Armand Fallières
6918edf0-4e2e-58b2-82d5-437119b828fa.description2: The Lycée Armand-Fallières, attended in his time by Jules Ferry and named after the President of the French Republic, was located on the Rue de Russie and had the objective of educating the daughters of European settlers in their secondary education. In the early 20th century, a few Tunisians began to attend the school and thus had access to a modern European education. This photograph shows a secondary school class of young girls.

69333e0f-47a7-51b4-ada7-d43aa30c07fe.name: Flag of the peasants’ league of a small village in Tuscany, central Italy
69333e0f-47a7-51b4-ada7-d43aa30c07fe.author: Giulia Barrera
69333e0f-47a7-51b4-ada7-d43aa30c07fe.archival: ACS, Partito nazionale fascista, Mostra della Rivoluzione fascista
69333e0f-47a7-51b4-ada7-d43aa30c07fe.description2:
Peasants’ leagues (Lega Contadina) were the first form of agricultural workers’ organisations. They flourished in Italy at the end of the nineteenth and beginning of the twentieth century.  
Ravi and Caldana are villages in the municipality of Gavorrano (a mine district in the province of Grosseto, Tuscany).  
In 1911, when the national trade union Confederazione Generale del Lavoro (CGdL) proclaimed a strike against Italy’s colonial war in Libya, the miners of the Gavorrano district participated in the strike.

695e33b8-130e-58a9-b5e3-7cf462619cb9.name: The School of the Three Doctors
695e33b8-130e-58a9-b5e3-7cf462619cb9.description: The School of the Three Doctors, pictured here, is located in Downtown Beirut. The inscription above the main entrance bears the school's full name and the date of its foundation (1835).
695e33b8-130e-58a9-b5e3-7cf462619cb9.author: Hala Masri
695e33b8-130e-58a9-b5e3-7cf462619cb9.history: The Three Doctors Association represented the Orthodox educational presence in 19th century Lebanon. The school was also known as the 'Grand School' as it was the biggest school in Beirut. It was temporarily closed from 1840 to 1860, and again during the civil war, from 1975 to 1998.

69c68c59-f8ea-58f9-8d04-9f7f7e1327d4.name: In the Sicilian Sulphur Mines
69c68c59-f8ea-58f9-8d04-9f7f7e1327d4.holder: State Library of Modern and Contemporary History
69c68c59-f8ea-58f9-8d04-9f7f7e1327d4.author: Giulia Barrera
69c68c59-f8ea-58f9-8d04-9f7f7e1327d4.second_name: Children at work in the Sicilian sulphur mines at the end of the 19th century
69c68c59-f8ea-58f9-8d04-9f7f7e1327d4.description2:
Sicilian sulphur mines at the end of the 19th century employed children as young as seven and eight years old to carry the crude ore up from the mines to the surface.  
In Italy, the first piece of law regarding children’s work dates back to 1886. It forbade employing children under the age of nine in factories and mines. It also dictated that children under the age of 12 could not work at night. Such provisions indicated the extremely hard situation of children workers at the time. Particularly appalling were the working conditions of children in the Sicilian sulphur mines. Their plight was highlighted by the Italian writer Giovanni Verga in his short story *Rosso Malpelo*, and by Nobel laureate Luigi Pirandello in his *Ciàula scopre la Luna*.

6c348586-1356-5ba4-b2b5-0c09d19282dc.name: The Victims of Labour
6c348586-1356-5ba4-b2b5-0c09d19282dc.author: Marina Minozzi
6c348586-1356-5ba4-b2b5-0c09d19282dc.keywords: Sculpture; Italian sculptors; realism; Verismo; social topics; post-unitarian Italian society; rights of workers; working class; life expectancy; poverty; industry; communication; industrial development; road; railway; international; universal exposition
6c348586-1356-5ba4-b2b5-0c09d19282dc.copyright: Copyright image: Soprintendenza alla Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Moderna e Contemporanea.
6c348586-1356-5ba4-b2b5-0c09d19282dc.description2: Vincenzo Vela studied at the academy of Fine arts of Brera and at the age of 22 he won an Academy of Venice competition. The artwork is an homage to the workers who died during the construction of the Gotthard Tunnel between 1872-82, which had implemented new cost-lowering techniques that also caused numerous incidents and loss of life. Work conditions were very unhealthy: temperatures over 30 degrees, gas exhalations and no air shafts. Even the accommodations were unhealthy and dirty. When the workers went on strike for the inhumane conditions, police shot at protesters, killing four workers. The miners in *The Victims of Labour* are depicted carrying the body of a dying classmate on a stretcher out of the tunnel. A self-portrait of the sculptor is recognisable in the classmate’s face. The harsh modelling of the workers’ bodies, almost deformed, makes the scene even more powerful. The artist affirmed he had no commission for this work which was a passion project. In 1895 it was cast in bronze on request of the Ministry of Education; in 1900 it was sent to the Universal Exhibition in Paris.

6cc37690-74bf-5956-9550-3a0a66b523c8.description: In 1914, the French Protectorate put forward a new policy to modernise the education system in Morocco. Integrating the new policy with the traditional education system, scholars (the *'ulama´*) of al-Qarawiyyin University modernised educational material while still respecting the old system.

707017b0-ac19-5968-8e9b-29b8a4f1aeab.name: Weighing armchair
707017b0-ac19-5968-8e9b-29b8a4f1aeab.description2: Weighing armchairs were used for medical purposes. Early metabolism studies were made by weighing the test subjects before and after eating or any other activities. They were also used to weigh handicapped people and old patients who could not stand up. The chair is made of polished brown walnut wood. There are two rows of metal plates in front of the seating area. There is a decoration made by punched holes on the backside of the armchair. There is a wooden footrest attached with metal bars to the main body of the armchair. On the rear side there is a weighing mechanism.

72aa413c-a02a-5412-a43e-1c63e804854f.name: École Sadiki
72aa413c-a02a-5412-a43e-1c63e804854f.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
72aa413c-a02a-5412-a43e-1c63e804854f.history: Built in 1875 by Sadok Pacha Bey's grand vizier the General Khaireddine (Khayr al-Din), l'École Sadiki was the first Tunisian school to introduce modern teaching and move away from a traditional religious education, a move characterised by the introduction of foregin languages and the mathematical and physical sciences. L'École Sadiki was a breeding ground for Tunisian intellectuals with a love for political protesting and Westernization.
72aa413c-a02a-5412-a43e-1c63e804854f.description2: Although its first home were disused barracks, the École Sadiki moved to its current building on top of the kasbah in Tunis in 1897. It was designed by the French architect Maillet in a typical Arab style, and thus has the grandeur of official French buildings whilst also using shapes from traditional Arab architecture. Built on two floors, its internal layout is similar to Western architecture, but it recalls the Arab medina in its external ornamental features and decor, with arches on marble columns and Turkish capitals, and with cupolas, green-tiled cornices etc.

73e736ab-49ec-5eea-8f27-af65046fe133.name: Headdress
73e736ab-49ec-5eea-8f27-af65046fe133.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
73e736ab-49ec-5eea-8f27-af65046fe133.author: Huda Kilani
73e736ab-49ec-5eea-8f27-af65046fe133.keywords: silver; prominent dome; disk; al- Druz women
73e736ab-49ec-5eea-8f27-af65046fe133.description2: A silver circular disk with filigree work and prominent dome above; chains dangling with triple petal and filigree work at the end; placed on the top of a high hat worn by al-Druze (Druse) women. Silver was the most common jewellery. The dowry of silver and gold jewellery was given by the groom to the bride, reflecting the financial status of the groom. This object illustrates the variegated social composition and the demographic changes in the Jordanian territory in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The al-Druze tribes migrated from Syria (Hawran) to north east Jordan in the early twentieth century because of their support for the Syrian revolution against the French occupation.

76a1492a-0881-5283-861f-8c45c2c06097.name: L'École de la Rue du Pacha (inside the classroom)
76a1492a-0881-5283-861f-8c45c2c06097.holder: Institut Supérieur d’Histoire Contemporaine de la Tunisie
76a1492a-0881-5283-861f-8c45c2c06097.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
76a1492a-0881-5283-861f-8c45c2c06097.description2: This photograph shows a classroom of young Muslim girls at l'École Louise-Renée-Millet (renamed l'École de la Rue du Pacha in 1911/1912) in 1908. The presence of a *moueddeb* and a French teacher is notable. The *moueddeb* would have taught the principles of the Quran and elementary Arabic (reading, writing, arithmetic), whereas the French teacher would have covered the French education (literature, history, science and hygiene), as well as needlework (embroidery, sewing, lace). For the younger pupils of the school this classroom was the door to the world and one which allowed them to explore life. Young girls of this time often lived very sheltered lives, shut away in their homes without the opportunity to learn. Their education was usually limited to housework and needlework, either at home or at a Dar el-Maalma, a local atelier run by an old housewife.

779c654a-aa90-53f1-a122-5dbb8e302070.name: *Interior of a school, Cairo*
779c654a-aa90-53f1-a122-5dbb8e302070.author: Victoria and Albert Museum
779c654a-aa90-53f1-a122-5dbb8e302070.keywords: education; school; teaching; children; childhood; kuttab
779c654a-aa90-53f1-a122-5dbb8e302070.description2: In this scene depicted by Lewis, the Hoja or teacher is listening to his assistant rhythmically reciting the Quran (while beating time), as some children pay attention and others not. Some commentators have regarded the presence of a young girl as inauthentic, but young girls were able to attend Quran schools, according to the artist Charles de Tournemine, the scholar Edward Lane and the translator Richard Burton. Certainly not all women were illiterate, and some female descendants of the prophet were noted for their ability to read and recite the scriptures.

77cb95e6-9ec9-5628-a3f9-c509f77d9e94.name: Astronomical Observatory of Lisbon Polytechnic School
77cb95e6-9ec9-5628-a3f9-c509f77d9e94.holder: National Museum of Natural History and Science (MUHNAC) / Museums of the University of Lisbon
77cb95e6-9ec9-5628-a3f9-c509f77d9e94.author: António Perestrelo de Matos (MUHNAC-UL)
77cb95e6-9ec9-5628-a3f9-c509f77d9e94.history: Teaching of Astronomy existed in the Lisbon Polytechnic School since its creation in 1837. It was aimed at providing training for cartography surveys. Initially, teaching was done at the so-called Marine Tower (1837–1843) and then at the Royal Maritime Observatory (1843–1875). In 1876, a new Observatory was inaugurated in the Garden. However, the first building had low stability and a new one had to be constructed. Astronomy teaching started in 1898. Until the 1930s, the Observatory was autonomous within the School, but later it was put under the jurisdiction of the Department of Mathematics. In 1999 teaching was discontinued and the Observatory was integrated in the Museum.
77cb95e6-9ec9-5628-a3f9-c509f77d9e94.keywords: Observatory; Scientific Heritage; Teaching; Astronomy; National Museum of Natural History and Science; University of Lisbon
77cb95e6-9ec9-5628-a3f9-c509f77d9e94.architects: Vitor Augusto Gomes da Encarnação (19th century) and José Cecílio da Costa (19th century)
77cb95e6-9ec9-5628-a3f9-c509f77d9e94.third_name: Observatório Astronómico da Escola Politécnica de Lisboa
77cb95e6-9ec9-5628-a3f9-c509f77d9e94.description2: The Astronomical Observatory is a teaching observatory. It includes one classroom and three observation domes. It dates from 1898 and it encompasses three buildings. The main building is octagonal in shape, located in the upper part of the Botanical Garden. Inside, it has a classroom and the Meridian Room, all covered in wood panels. Another building, with three-floors, used to host the library, more classrooms and workshops. The Observatory collection includes c. 150 scientific instruments, including several apparatuses built in house by Portuguese astronomer Campos Rodrigues (1836–1919).

7becfe40-aaa5-590f-a2a3-17c23dfb1f52.name: *Faculty of Medicine First Year Students*
7becfe40-aaa5-590f-a2a3-17c23dfb1f52.keywords: Education; Students; Faculty of Medicine; Egyptian University
7becfe40-aaa5-590f-a2a3-17c23dfb1f52.description2: Photograph of first year Faculty of Medicine students at Egyptian University. The 1923 Constitution stipulated that “Primary education is mandatory for all Egyptian boys and girls”. A decree was issued for the establishment of a public university under the name “The Egyptian University” in 1925, comprised of four faculties; literature, science, medicine and law. The Faculty of Medicine, annexed to Qasr al-`Ayni Hospital, is one of the leading hospitals in the Arab World.

7f8a48e3-b8ea-55d5-9114-484b7cc5c0a2.name: *Thymus ciliatus* Benth. Presently: *Thymus munbyanus* subsp. coloratus (Boiss. & Reut.) Greuter & Burdet

7f8a48e3-b8ea-55d5-9114-484b7cc5c0a2.keywords: Herbarium; vascular plant; aromatic; North Africa; National Museum of Natural History and Science; University of Lisbon
7f8a48e3-b8ea-55d5-9114-484b7cc5c0a2.materials: Pressed and dried plant, glued on paper
7f8a48e3-b8ea-55d5-9114-484b7cc5c0a2.description2: Natural History Museums were an important institution for scientific researching, exchange and circulate ideas and natural knowledge. This object is a Herbarium and the specimen was collected in Algeria, on the Lions Mountain, near Oran, in May 1850 by Giles Munby. The aromatic leaves are grey-green, covered with hairs. The pink flowers are crowded into terminal clusters. It is a drought tolerant species from NW Africa (Algeria and Morocco). It is included in the first Centuria of Plantae Algeriensis Exciccatae, distributed to different herbaria. It is used as a medicinal plant in its area of occurrence.
