83550dcd-d5fe-53bf-ba81-33534dbf86ed.name: Lace skirt
83550dcd-d5fe-53bf-ba81-33534dbf86ed.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
83550dcd-d5fe-53bf-ba81-33534dbf86ed.author: Huda Kilani
83550dcd-d5fe-53bf-ba81-33534dbf86ed.description2: Skirt of light pink lace with black flowers, pursed from the middle, worn over a woman’s dress. This object illustrates the variegated population composition of Jordan in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, the various local costumes and rites, fashion and personal attire. This skirt was used by al-Druze women in Jordan. The al-Druze tribes migrated from Syria (Hawran) to north east Jordan in the early twentieth century because of their support for the Syrian revolution against the French occupation.

874efcbf-3d66-55db-9523-6302edc55a76.name: Institut Pasteur
874efcbf-3d66-55db-9523-6302edc55a76.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
874efcbf-3d66-55db-9523-6302edc55a76.history: l'Institut Pasteur de Tunis, created in 1893 by the nephew of Louis Pasteur, Adrien Loir, was the third Institut Pasteur in the world after Paris and Hanoi (now Ho-Chi-Minh City), and one of the 32 Institut Pasteur centres scattered around the world. The institute aims to provide a pioneering health service in the field of prevention, prophylaxis and cutting-edge research. Its prestige can also be attributed to the doctor Charles Nicolle, who was the director between 1903 and 1936 and discovered the typhus virus during his time there. l'Institut Pasteur played a decisive role in the fight against certain illnesses, such as rabies. It remains today an important national and international reference centre for many illnesses.
874efcbf-3d66-55db-9523-6302edc55a76.keywords: Charles Nicolle; Institut Pasteur; Nobel prize
874efcbf-3d66-55db-9523-6302edc55a76.description2: Initially a rabies vaccine centre, this building then became a general vaccination centre and finally an analysis laboratory. It is located at the crossroads named Place Pasteur, not far from the old European quarter, and eventually expanded from three, to nine, to eighteen laboratories. One of its biggest missions was concerned with diagnosis and public health, another with the production of vaccines and serums, and a third concentrated on research, development and innovation. The research clinic matched patients to clinical trials and worked in coordination with the various different laboratories and research teams.

888046f7-3ef2-5941-9017-769431669b16.name: Ring
888046f7-3ef2-5941-9017-769431669b16.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
888046f7-3ef2-5941-9017-769431669b16.author: Huda Kilani
888046f7-3ef2-5941-9017-769431669b16.keywords: Floral decoration; religious objects; waqf; Qur’an; Ottoman Baroque-Rococo
888046f7-3ef2-5941-9017-769431669b16.description2:
Thin silver ring with a squared black stone set in silver. Silver jewellery was the most common, because only rich people could afford gold jewellery. The dowry of silver and gold jewellery was given by the groom to the bride, reflecting the financial status of the groom.  
Jordan's economy in the late 19th and early 20th centuries relied on trades and crafts and new waves of people started to come to Jordan and began to settle for this purpose. This object is an example of how traditional fashion reflected the variegated population composition of Jordan in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It is also an example of local personal attire, fashion, costumes and rites.

88f4e317-6501-5591-b5b3-41a03b3515d2.name: *Strike fund*
88f4e317-6501-5591-b5b3-41a03b3515d2.description2: "Strike funds" were established during strikes, collecting money which they received from donations and subscription fees. These funds are able to financially support strikers, who no longer received their salaries and therefore had no means of survival. This drawing emphasises the anxiety on the faces of the workers and their families, who relied wholly on this solidarity for their food and lodgings. It also mocks the role of the Minister of the Interior, who was sending in military troops instead of funds. Indeed, many strikes were interrupted by the arrival of military forces between 1899 and 1901.

89b9e8c6-f3d0-5b3f-8890-c5a4ed5ba8cf.name: Dreams
89b9e8c6-f3d0-5b3f-8890-c5a4ed5ba8cf.author: Marina Minozzi
89b9e8c6-f3d0-5b3f-8890-c5a4ed5ba8cf.keywords: Realism; Italian painters; social topics; post-unitarian Italian society; woman; women's condition; women's rights; social changes; education; women's education; literacy; illiteracy; fashion; international exhibitions; international exposition
89b9e8c6-f3d0-5b3f-8890-c5a4ed5ba8cf.copyright: Copyright image: Soprintendenza alla Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Moderna e Contemporanea.
89b9e8c6-f3d0-5b3f-8890-c5a4ed5ba8cf.description2: Vittorio Corcos is well known for his realistic paintings, especially his portraits of women. The woman depicted in the painting *Dreams* is Elena Vecchi, the daughter of a friend of the painter. Elena spent her adolescence at Corcos’ home. Presented in 1897 at the International Exposition Art of Florence, the portrait drew great attention and critical and public acclaim. Given the subject and its allusive title, it’s possible to see the image of a modern, proud and aware young woman that hitherto was represented only in literature: on the contrary, Corcos was able to masterfully represent it in painting. The scene was so admired that it was also reproduced on postcards. Corcos believed that while a portrait of a man has to show his social status, that of a woman always has to be appealing even if she is eighty years old.

8a6b8745-c790-5c63-ae1c-ad2221823d69.description2: An influenza epidemic swept through Europe after the First World War, killing millions of those who had been weakened by the war. Many failed attempts were made distribute preventative medicines, like in this English school.

8a6cfa46-5a45-55b6-8e98-9c89d191db94.name: Primary students at a village school in central Italy, which followed the teaching methods introduced by Maria Montessori
8a6cfa46-5a45-55b6-8e98-9c89d191db94.author: Giulia Barrera
8a6cfa46-5a45-55b6-8e98-9c89d191db94.archival: Collezione tessile di Tela Umbra, Fondo fotografico
8a6cfa46-5a45-55b6-8e98-9c89d191db94.description2:
When Italy became a nation state in 1861, the illiteracy rate in the country was 78 per cent. In 1901, it was still at 56 per cent. Illiteracy was particularly high in the countryside. In 1877, the “Coppino Law”, made elementary schools mandatory and free of charge.  
Maria Montessori (1870-1952) was a medical doctor who developed innovative teaching methods for primary-school children. Her educational methods were first applied in the first decade of the 20th century. They met with great success and were applied in thousands of schools all over Europe and North America.

8b529731-afad-5c0e-8816-7664ae89852a.name: Lithographed Qur’an, originally written by Shukr Zadeh (d. AH 1166 / AD 1753)
8b529731-afad-5c0e-8816-7664ae89852a.holder: Sharjah Museum of Islamic Civilisation / Sharjah Museums Department
8b529731-afad-5c0e-8816-7664ae89852a.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
8b529731-afad-5c0e-8816-7664ae89852a.artist: Original calligraphed by Shukr Zadeh (d. AH 1166 / AD 1753)
8b529731-afad-5c0e-8816-7664ae89852a.description2: This Qur'an, originally caligraphed by the famous Ottoman calligrapher Shukr Zadeh is the first Qur'an to be printed in an Islamic country by way of lithograpy. It was produced around 1850 AD.While printing had begun in Europe many centuries ago, the Islamic world continued to favour handwritten books, and most certainly as regards copies of the Holy Qur’an. In 1834, the first edition of Gustav Fluegel’s printed Qur’an was published, while in the Ottoman Empire, the printing of Qur’ans began only in the second half of the 19th century, both in Egypt and in Istanbul. Most were lithographed, as they had the look and feel of manuscripts. Most importantly, all the required recitational signs could be rendered accurately.

8b77b70b-784c-5988-890e-779ea486c18e.name: Letter by the Prefect of Cosenza (Calabria, Italy) to the Ministry of Agriculture, Industry and Trade, referring to the exceedingly long working hours of women and children in the spinning factories
8b77b70b-784c-5988-890e-779ea486c18e.author: Margherita Martino
8b77b70b-784c-5988-890e-779ea486c18e.archival: ASCS, Prefettura, Affari generali, categoria 7, b. 523
8b77b70b-784c-5988-890e-779ea486c18e.description2: In Italy, the first law that introduced some forms of protection for female workers was approved in 1902 (l. 242/1902). It limited the working hours for women to 12 hours a day and introduced a one-month maternity leave after delivery. When this letter was written, there was a discussion in the country on the possible regulation of the working conditions of women and children. The Prefect of Cosenza reported that there were factories in which women and children worked from 4:30 in the morning to 10:30 at night.

8c5bd2b7-5767-58df-9aca-d0fdbe20c4ea.name: Portable pharmacy
8c5bd2b7-5767-58df-9aca-d0fdbe20c4ea.author: Paula Basso
8c5bd2b7-5767-58df-9aca-d0fdbe20c4ea.description2: The Arab world was a territory to discover but with a individual pharmacy travel case in order to face different diseases.

8d188108-655f-550e-b130-a0eb24f32b9c.name: Headdress
8d188108-655f-550e-b130-a0eb24f32b9c.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
8d188108-655f-550e-b130-a0eb24f32b9c.author: Huda Kilani
8d188108-655f-550e-b130-a0eb24f32b9c.description2: Three bands of silver (800) chain fitted around the sides and over the crown of the head; 1/4 Ottoman coins (*barah*s) are fixed in the inner section of the band. This kind of jewellery was part of the dowry the groom gave to the bride. Dowries consisted mostly of silver jewellery because only the rich could afford gold jewellery. Thus, the financial status of the groom was highlighted by the jewellery he could give as a dowry and by the use of coins as pieces of jewellery for his wife.

8efde259-472d-50ce-9578-75e8ff556e35.name: *Nosocomium* \[Latin: Hospital\]
8efde259-472d-50ce-9578-75e8ff556e35.author: Marina Minozzi
8efde259-472d-50ce-9578-75e8ff556e35.keywords: Italian painters; city; urban space; segregation; medicine; disease; poverty; illness; life expectancy; psychiatry; social changes; scientific development; social topics; post-unitarian Italian society; Positivism; celebration of science; exposition
8efde259-472d-50ce-9578-75e8ff556e35.copyright: Copyright image: Soprintendenza alla Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Moderna e Contemporanea.
8efde259-472d-50ce-9578-75e8ff556e35.description2: Silvio Rotta was introduced to painting by his father and, in his early years, produced mainly watercolours, genre compositions inspired by Venetian popular customs. In 1887, after an illness, the production of the artist underwent a radical change ad began to show social realism through the depiction of the insane. *Nosocomium* represents a psychiatric hospital where poor and sick were hosted and nursed. The scale of the canvas is accentuated by the diagonal of the benches and the path. The painting won awards at the 1895 Biennale of Venice and is now recognised as one of the most important works by Rotta. The scene’s realism offers a merciless analysis and public complaint about the patients’ living conditions. Caring of poor and sick was an important issue during the 19th century and a law to control hospitals and mental institution was discussed in those years.

8f1ec06d-13b0-5253-b0bf-a8afb87b0260.description2: Learning to write in Quranic schools took place by copying verses of the Quran onto slabs, which were then carefully erased.

91a520f6-9937-54cd-a224-0a3b83e3587f.name: Azurite
91a520f6-9937-54cd-a224-0a3b83e3587f.holder: National Museum of Natural History and Science (MUHNAC) / Museums of the University of Lisbon
91a520f6-9937-54cd-a224-0a3b83e3587f.author: Liliana Póvoas (MUHNAC-UL)
91a520f6-9937-54cd-a224-0a3b83e3587f.keywords: Azurite; carbonate mineral; monoclinic system; copper; pigment; jewellery; National Museum of Natural History and Science; University of Lisbon
91a520f6-9937-54cd-a224-0a3b83e3587f.description2: Two aggregates of azurite prismatic crystals with a radial distribution. Azurite is a copper carbonate mineral, of chemical formula Cu3(CO3)2(OH)2. Its name comes from the antiquity for its deep blue colour after the Arabian azure that came from the Persian lazhward. Azurite crystals conform to the monoclinic system of symmetry. In this sample they are prismatic, opaque and their faces present striations. The lustre is vitreous. Azurite was used as a blue pigment for centuries, providing a wide range of blues. It is also used as jewellery and as an ornamental stone. As a secondary mineral found in the oxidized portions of copper deposits, the presence of Azurite is a good surface indicator of the presence of copper ores. This sample was collected at the Touissit Mine, near Oudja, Morocco.
91a520f6-9937-54cd-a224-0a3b83e3587f.holding_institution_org: Museu Nacional da Historia Natural e da Ciencia (MUHNAC)

922ac1b0-e425-5db9-98ed-2ceda9b73f82.name: Zaytuna University
922ac1b0-e425-5db9-98ed-2ceda9b73f82.holder: Institut Supérieur d’Histoire Contemporaine de la Tunisie
922ac1b0-e425-5db9-98ed-2ceda9b73f82.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
922ac1b0-e425-5db9-98ed-2ceda9b73f82.description2: This photograph shows young students coming out of a class in the Zaytuna University. In fact, the mosque was not only a place of worship, but also a sizeable university. A number of theologians, litterateurs, and art and science scholars from all over the Arab world (with an emphasis on North Africa) founded, across various generations, the Zaytuna university in Tunis. The teaching was constantly being modernized and restructured during the 19th century, and particularly under the reign of Ahmed Pacha Bey and the viziership of the reforming minister Khaireddine (Khayr al-Din).

962e3954-6b7a-5ffb-a881-c31a4aa6530a.name: The Benefits of Hygiene. Hydrotherapy
962e3954-6b7a-5ffb-a881-c31a4aa6530a.holder: Archivio unico regionale di deposito – Solomeo di Corciano
962e3954-6b7a-5ffb-a881-c31a4aa6530a.author: Giulia Barrera
962e3954-6b7a-5ffb-a881-c31a4aa6530a.archival: Archivio Opera pia regina Margherita Fondazione Franchetti di Città di Castello, Scuole di Montesca e di Rovigliano, Elaborati degli alunni, Quaderni, album ed esercitazioni, b. 1, fasc. 3
962e3954-6b7a-5ffb-a881-c31a4aa6530a.second_name: Notebook used by a third-grade student in a village school in Central Italy, in 1908–1909
962e3954-6b7a-5ffb-a881-c31a4aa6530a.description2:
In Italy, the first law that introduced compulsory education (the so-called “Coppino law”) dates back to 1877. Only the first three years of elementary school were compulsory. In 1911, the law extended compulsory education up to the age of 12.  
During the 19th century, illiteracy in Italy was very high: in 1867, almost 70 per cent of spouses who could not sign their marriage certificate because were unable to write; in 1901, there were still about 39 per cent of spouses who could not sign their marriage certificate.

96b87e45-a0fc-5ed9-baea-de7b25724cf7.name: *Maktab al-\`Anbar School, Damascus*
96b87e45-a0fc-5ed9-baea-de7b25724cf7.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum, State Museums
96b87e45-a0fc-5ed9-baea-de7b25724cf7.author: Stefan Weber
96b87e45-a0fc-5ed9-baea-de7b25724cf7.second_name: First modern secondary school founded by the state in Damascus. Building was originally a private dwelling
96b87e45-a0fc-5ed9-baea-de7b25724cf7.description2: The growth of Damascus urban culture and the changing role of the state were accompanied by important reforms and social changes. One of them was an increased alphabetisation and an improved public education. Attempts were first made by the state to reform schools in 1869 with the passing of an edict on school reform for the whole Ottoman Empire, officially recognizing private and foreign schools while setting out the basic principles of state education. The law now made a distinction between military schools on the one hand, and schools preparing children for a civil service or administrative career on the other hand. An example for the latter is Maktab al-`Anbar school.

9863f692-894f-5cb2-b496-b0ec25aba740.name: Kabyle mother with her child
9863f692-894f-5cb2-b496-b0ec25aba740.description2: Western photographers were particularly interested in both women's daily lives, and family life. This photo from 1920 shows a Kabyle woman carrying her baby with a look of pride on her face.

98dd6374-5559-5f34-9752-bbdb0e9ee65a.name: Class photograph in Tartej
98dd6374-5559-5f34-9752-bbdb0e9ee65a.author: Hala Masri
98dd6374-5559-5f34-9752-bbdb0e9ee65a.description2: This photograph was taken in Tartij, a village in the Mount Lebanon district. The sign behind the children reads "*Vive L'Académie Tartej (Liban)*" (Long Live Tartij Academy (Lebanon)). The young boys on the far sides are wearing traditional baggy trousers called *shirwal*. The younger boys underneath the sign are barefoot.

9aa9bf06-9414-5502-8c25-a49ce6269462.name: Belt
9aa9bf06-9414-5502-8c25-a49ce6269462.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
9aa9bf06-9414-5502-8c25-a49ce6269462.author: Huda Kilani
9aa9bf06-9414-5502-8c25-a49ce6269462.description2: A Circassian belt with 15 silver and niello-decorated buckles connected together to form the belt; there is a rosette shape at the end with locking mechanism and three dangling silver tassels. This belt, together with the dagger, was an accessory forming the traditional male Circassian dress. The Circassians used to carry daggers which were an essential part of the national dress. The immigration of the Circassians to the Ottoman Empire started in the middle of 19th century and continued until 1900. The Circassian communities migrated mostly to the eastern Arab countries with which they had spiritual and religious links.

9b0fa536-0fe5-5f95-ba19-41b4f81e9fd4.name: Brass head of flagpole
9b0fa536-0fe5-5f95-ba19-41b4f81e9fd4.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
9b0fa536-0fe5-5f95-ba19-41b4f81e9fd4.author: Huda Kilani
9b0fa536-0fe5-5f95-ba19-41b4f81e9fd4.description2: This mast, made of casted brass, bears an Arabic calligraphic decoration with the inscription "Oh God, Oh Muhammad". It is fixed on a pointed piece of copper with a hole at the bottom to install on a long wooden staff. In religious festivities such as a pilgrimage, various activities were organized. They would normally include festivals and rallies under flags and standards. The heads of flagstaffs were decorated with metallic items usually with Arabic calligraphy and some cosmic signs such as the crescent and the star.

9b7f13f5-9188-59a0-bf2d-8b4f7c9b66cb.name: Brass head of flagpole
9b7f13f5-9188-59a0-bf2d-8b4f7c9b66cb.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
9b7f13f5-9188-59a0-bf2d-8b4f7c9b66cb.author: Huda Kilani
9b7f13f5-9188-59a0-bf2d-8b4f7c9b66cb.description2: A cultic item with Arabic calligraphy mentioning God and his prophet Muhammad made of casted brass; fixed on a pointed piece of copper with a hole at the bottom to install on a long wooden staff. In religious festivities such as a pilgrimage, various activities were organized that would normally include festivals and rallies under flags and standards. The heads of flagstaffs were decorated with metallic items usually with Arabic calligraphy and some cosmic signs such as the crescent and the star.

9c2ac3c9-ddf9-5578-9e26-fad8ec3a615c.name: Dhow collection
9c2ac3c9-ddf9-5578-9e26-fad8ec3a615c.keywords: Boat; ship; dhow; pearling; fishing; trade; transportation
9c2ac3c9-ddf9-5578-9e26-fad8ec3a615c.description2: The National Museum of Qatar holds, in its collection, a fleet comprising of 14 dhows. The growing collection includes a variety of traditional dhows, with several models dating to the early 20th century, as well as more recent replicas of traditional vessels. Originating from Oman, Bahrayn, India and Qatar, among other places traditional dhows represented include *jalbut* (small to medium sized), *shuw\`i* (medium sized, once used for fishing and coastal trade), *sanbuq* (largest type in the Arabian Gulf today) and *baglah* (traditional, deep-sea dhows once used for the long – haul transport of goods.)

9e4b0c24-5146-5cba-abc0-63ecdffbe58d.name: Portrait of Labiba Geahchan
9e4b0c24-5146-5cba-abc0-63ecdffbe58d.holder: 'Zahrat al-Ihsan School ('The Flower of Beneficence' School)

9e8a7ea8-8f60-59b4-af77-1fef1a414d6a.name: Construction of the Aswan Dam
9e8a7ea8-8f60-59b4-af77-1fef1a414d6a.description2:
Photograph showing labourers during the construction of the Aswan Dam gates.  
Located in Upper Egypt, the Aswan Dam was the first water storage project in modern times.

9f4dd257-a6bc-5852-b6b1-45af52c3e4f7.name: Military Medical kit of Carol Davila
9f4dd257-a6bc-5852-b6b1-45af52c3e4f7.description2: In the second half of the 19th century, French doctor Carol Davila played an important role in the development of the Romanian medical system. He came to Bucharest in 1853, sent by the French government at the request of Wallachian prince Barbu Stirbei who needed a specialist to form well trained Romanian doctors. Davila was named medic of the army and later general inspector of the country’s sanitary service and he was the founder of a medicine and pharmacy school. Among other decorations he received for his activity, he was awarded two Ottoman ones (the Orders of Medjidie and of Osmanie), the first for curing Ottoman soldiers who contracted cholera during the Ottoman occupation of Wallachia (1855), and the other for treating wounded Ottoman soldiers during the Russian-Ottoman war of 1877-1878.

a0ae7c32-123a-5f92-8eb4-161510e42915.name: 'Zahrat Al-Ihsan School
a0ae7c32-123a-5f92-8eb4-161510e42915.description: A view of the modern building of Zahrat al-Ihsan school, one of the most renowned Lebanese charitable institutions founded in the nineteenth century to provide education for young girls in Beirut.
a0ae7c32-123a-5f92-8eb4-161510e42915.author: Hala Masri
a0ae7c32-123a-5f92-8eb4-161510e42915.history: This school was founded by two sisters, Mary Geahchan and Ms Emilie Sursuq. The construction was funded by the donations from the Orthodox Church and first opened on 30 August 1881. Whilst it was originally a school for orphan girls, it later became a private school and became co-educational during the 1975-1990 Lebanese Civil War.

a1f0d2c4-ed0e-520e-ae95-52264d8e107d.name: The patients in Darülaceze Hospital
a1f0d2c4-ed0e-520e-ae95-52264d8e107d.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)
a1f0d2c4-ed0e-520e-ae95-52264d8e107d.keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph; hospital; health
a1f0d2c4-ed0e-520e-ae95-52264d8e107d.description2: One of the world's largest photo archives, Abdülhamid II's photo archives – knows as the Yildiz Albums – contain about 37 thousand pictures from that period of the Ottoman Empire. The photo archives contain images of cities, buildings which were built by sultan, schools, students, soldiers, mosques, ports, government departments, shipyards, railways, bridges, bazaars, machines, locomotives and factories. Darülaceze Hospital was established in Okmeydanı, Istanbul İn 1895 on the instructions of Abdülhamid II for the care of elderly, homeless and disabled people in need.

a417f6af-5483-5922-be43-098a03e3261f.name: *Algiers, site of the Lycée*
a417f6af-5483-5922-be43-098a03e3261f.author: Dalila Orfali
a417f6af-5483-5922-be43-098a03e3261f.description2: This building was home to the first French educational institution in Algiers, as indicated by its name "Lycée". It was built on the site of an ancient columbarium, not far from where the deys' tombs had been prior to their demolition and the construction of Bab el-Oued esplanade. It was constructed under the direction of the architect Frédéric Chassériau, although the archaeologist Adrien Berbrugger organised excavations before the works began. Today, it is called Lycée Émir Abdelkader, and remains one of the most important scholarly institutions in the city.

a46e70b6-0a07-57b9-ad2a-d974179b2424.name: Water jug
a46e70b6-0a07-57b9-ad2a-d974179b2424.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
a46e70b6-0a07-57b9-ad2a-d974179b2424.author: Huda Kilani
a46e70b6-0a07-57b9-ad2a-d974179b2424.description2: A copper circular-shaped ewer with a very narrow neck, arched handle and strait long nozzle, used in mosques of Jordan and Palestine to wash before praying. This is another example of how the same objects, traditions, and activities were common in territories that now belong to different Arab states. In the late 19th century and early 20th century, there were still no boundaries between the Arab states and this – together with the lack of geographical barriers – made population movements, nomadism and migration a common factor influencing the everyday life and exchanges in the local society. The local economy, which relied heavily on trade and crafts, depended also on travel and migration in order to sell products or find markets for craft products.

a47e2724-6e4b-5b5c-ad40-f8e2d5e40ecb.name: Women working in a textile factory in Città di Castello (central Italy) at the beginning of the 20th century
a47e2724-6e4b-5b5c-ad40-f8e2d5e40ecb.author: Giulia Barrera
a47e2724-6e4b-5b5c-ad40-f8e2d5e40ecb.archival: Collezione tessile di Tela Umbra, Fondo fotografico
a47e2724-6e4b-5b5c-ad40-f8e2d5e40ecb.description2: At the beginning of the 20th century, textile factories in Italy employed a high proportion of female workers.

a73e56c5-c169-5488-aff8-8af1170f4be3.name: “The conqueror of Europe”
a73e56c5-c169-5488-aff8-8af1170f4be3.holder: State Library of Modern and Contemporary History
a73e56c5-c169-5488-aff8-8af1170f4be3.author: Giulia Barrera
a73e56c5-c169-5488-aff8-8af1170f4be3.second_name: A cartoon on the influenza pandemic of 1918, known as the “Spanish flu”
a73e56c5-c169-5488-aff8-8af1170f4be3.description2:
In Italy, the pandemic of influenza of 1918, known as “Spanish flu,” caused about 600,000 deaths out of a population of about 40 million. Around the world, it caused around 20 million deaths.  
The name derived from the fact that Spain – which did not participate in WWI – unlike other Western countries did not have press censorship, and so the news regarding the epidemic made headlines on newspapers. However, the epidemic did not start in Spain, but in China, then spread to the USA and arrived in Europe involuntarily carried by the US soldiers dispatched overseas.  
It hit particularly hard because the population was weakened by the hardships caused by the war and many medical doctors had been drafted, leaving civilians with insufficient medical assistance.
a73e56c5-c169-5488-aff8-8af1170f4be3.holding_institution_org: Biblioteca di Storia Moderna e Contemporanea

a8214078-f56a-5069-864a-a169981878ac.name: The archbishop Tubia Aoun
a8214078-f56a-5069-864a-a169981878ac.author: Hala Masri
a8214078-f56a-5069-864a-a169981878ac.description2: Pictured here is the archbishop Tubia Aoun

a8683bd7-cbf6-5821-a911-6ea63acae710.name: The Khaldouniya
a8683bd7-cbf6-5821-a911-6ea63acae710.holder: Institut Supérieur d’Histoire Contemporaine de la Tunisie
a8683bd7-cbf6-5821-a911-6ea63acae710.author: Bechir Yazidi
a8683bd7-cbf6-5821-a911-6ea63acae710.description2: Founded in Tunis on 22 December 1896, this school can be best described as a sort of modern school. Today, it houses a bilingual library holding several thousand volumes and hundreds of manuscripts, attached to the Bibliothèque Nationale de Tunisie. Founded by the Young Tunisians (Harakat al-Shabab al-Tunisi) and directed by Béchir Sfar, the school's name is a direct reference to the great Arab thinker Ibn Khaldoun. It had the aim of disseminating scientific and practical knowledge in the Arab cultural sphere, particularly among the students of the Zaytuna Mosque, whose teachings were considered archaic and purely religious. The institution was built near the Zaytuna thanks to the support of the French Resident-General, René Millet, who drew up its regulations and in so doing notably failed to include political and religious discussions, choosing instead to focus on encouraging critical and reflective thinking.

a96d4c0a-5e74-5015-a893-8254aa4f6dbd.name: Quranic school
a96d4c0a-5e74-5015-a893-8254aa4f6dbd.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
a96d4c0a-5e74-5015-a893-8254aa4f6dbd.description2: Pictured here is a school using traditional teaching methods - a Quranic school or a *kouttab*. The students are seated in a circle on mats on the floor of a sparsely decorated room around their teacher, the *moueddeb*. In the 19th century and early 20th centuries, the Quranic schools were a fundamental part of traditional education, where students would learn the Quran, Islamic thought and the basic rules of the Arabic language.

aba67976-e763-523c-b6b8-d3d8d4b775b6.name: Spread from lithographic-printed publication
aba67976-e763-523c-b6b8-d3d8d4b775b6.description: Despite Arabic lithographic printing arriving late to Morocco, the government did its best to catch up and printed a considerable number of books in all disciplines.
aba67976-e763-523c-b6b8-d3d8d4b775b6.keywords: Printing; lithograph; book; manuscript; social changes; technical innovation; literacy; illiteracy

ac642d3b-bbff-52e1-97f4-243c52c3dde5.holder: Archivio unico regionale di deposito – Solomeo di Corciano

ac642d3b-bbff-52e1-97f4-243c52c3dde5.second_name: A teacher disciplining a student (from an Italian textbook for second grade children)
ac642d3b-bbff-52e1-97f4-243c52c3dde5.description2: When Italy became a nation state in 1861, the illiteracy rate in the country was 78 per cent. Illiteracy was particularly high in the countryside. In 1877, the “Coppino Law”, made three years of elementary school mandatory and free of charge.

acfa76a9-edd6-5f50-bcf6-fef161aa398e.name: *Catholic mission to Brazzaville: freeing enchained slaves at Saint-Louis d'Oubangui*
acfa76a9-edd6-5f50-bcf6-fef161aa398e.keywords: Education; missionaries; abolition of slavery; confessional schools; Congo
acfa76a9-edd6-5f50-bcf6-fef161aa398e.description2: Despite the abolition of the slave trade in 1848, slavery continued to exist in 19th century Congo in other forms. Missionaries went to Congo with the aim of freeing these slaves, partly for ethical reasons but partly also in the hope of converting them, and often by buying them first with their own special funds.

ae4f06c1-8888-5c57-81c6-70d929b50897.name: *Nişan-ı Maarif* (Badge of Education)
ae4f06c1-8888-5c57-81c6-70d929b50897.description2: The owner of this medallion was Dr. Mustafa Münif Pasha (1855-1937), who was the founder and director of the Turkish School of Pharmacy, Dentistry, Midwives and Nurses. He worked as an assistant in the anatomy department starting in 1881. Later, he gave classes on surgery. In 1886 he gave courses on midwifery. This medallion (*Nişan- Maarif*) was given to teachers who were successful in science and art. On the front of the medallion, on the left there are olive tree leaves enamelled in green and yellow while on the right we see oak leaves. Those two forms a crescent on top for the ribbon. On the lower part the leaves merge with a pink ribbon pattern. In the middle of the medallion there is a *tuğra* of Mehmed Reşad V. (1909–1918) on red enamelled background. Around the *tuğra* (monogram) there is an inscription that reads, “*ulûm ve fünûn ve sanayi'-i nefîse*” (sciences and knowledge and fine arts).

aef7807d-0cef-5b06-ba3e-6be4aa40ba9c.name: Turkish woman
aef7807d-0cef-5b06-ba3e-6be4aa40ba9c.description2: The Zangaki brothers were a pair of photographers working in Egypt who sold "Orientalist" photos to Western tourists, allowing them to immortalise their trip to the "Orient". This photograph shows a young Turkish woman.

b09ea51a-72ba-5a0c-8a5d-88c708d9a1fa.name: Women going about their daily life
b09ea51a-72ba-5a0c-8a5d-88c708d9a1fa.holder: Institut Supérieur d’Histoire Contemporaine de la Tunisie
b09ea51a-72ba-5a0c-8a5d-88c708d9a1fa.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
b09ea51a-72ba-5a0c-8a5d-88c708d9a1fa.description2: In the eary 20th century the Tunisian woman, like her counterparts around the world, led a difficult life of hard work and exclusion from public life which was considered a man's world. Although it is important to take into account the variety of women's circumstances and experiences, depending on their background, it was nonetheless rare for a Tunisian woman at this time to have access to religious sciences, Arabic literature and even less so to the physical and mathematical sciences. The era of the great female poets, litterateurs and arts advocates in Kairouan had long passed. However a debate surrounding women's education was opening up in Tunisia, and particularly in Egypt, which presented women's education as a essential to the emancipation of society.

b0e2dccd-96c5-50e2-b106-1f6ac20db945.name: Portait of a Lebanese boy
b0e2dccd-96c5-50e2-b106-1f6ac20db945.author: Hala Masri
b0e2dccd-96c5-50e2-b106-1f6ac20db945.description2: Pictured here is a small Lebanese boy, standing next to a board which reads "*La France, Louis Khoury*" (France, Louis Khoury).

b588456d-6066-57a5-856e-b4b1770386d5.name: Plaster cast panel for microbiological education
b588456d-6066-57a5-856e-b4b1770386d5.description2: Maquettes were used in medical education in the Ottoman Empire before a western education system was adopted. The maquettes were commissioned abroad and before working on cadavers, models and moulages were used in classes. Maquettes prepared by Dr. Auzoux in Paris were first taken to Marseilles in boxes, then shipped to İstanbul from there. This example was made of plaster and contains examples of amoeba. There are Roman numerals under each example. On the lower left of the panel one can read "Établissements Auzoux, Rue de Vaugirard, Paris”.

b72f10b9-2459-52a4-9f0f-f0a69230148a.name: Five piasters
b72f10b9-2459-52a4-9f0f-f0a69230148a.description: On the obverse: "*'amara bi-ta'amul al-husayn bin 'ali 1338 'abduhu wa ibn 'abdihi*" (It is ordered to deal with by al-Hussein bin 'Ali 1334, God servant). On the reverse: "*al-hukuma al-'arabiyya al-hashimiyya / 'ishruna / hashimi / qurushan / duriba bi-makka al-mukarrama sana 8*" (Five piasters of Arab Hashemite Government, minted at Makka al-Mukarrama in reign year 8).
b72f10b9-2459-52a4-9f0f-f0a69230148a.author: Aida Naghawi
b72f10b9-2459-52a4-9f0f-f0a69230148a.keywords: Hussein bin Ali; five piasters; Arab Hashemite Government; Mecca; Hijaz; coin; coinage; currency; numismatics

b7d0545b-be32-5c47-ab91-272824042882.name: Headdress
b7d0545b-be32-5c47-ab91-272824042882.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
b7d0545b-be32-5c47-ab91-272824042882.author: Huda Kilani
b7d0545b-be32-5c47-ab91-272824042882.description2: Line of silver Ottoman coins sewn together on a piece of fabric, part of a headdress. This kind of jewellery was part of the dowry the groom gave to the bride. Dowries consisted mostly of silver jewellery because only the rich could afford gold jewellery. The use of coins as pieces of jewellery in particular was an indirect statement of the financial status of the groom, as brides wore those pieces of jewellery in front of relatives and friends.

b84ae82c-3c44-5a73-ae00-06a543d2035b.name: Dr Béchir Denguezli, doctoral thesis in medicine
b84ae82c-3c44-5a73-ae00-06a543d2035b.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
b84ae82c-3c44-5a73-ae00-06a543d2035b.description2: Pictured here is the cover of a doctoral thesis in medicine, written by Béchir Denguezli at l’Université de Bordeaux in 1897. Dr Béchir Denguezli was the first Tunisian doctor to study at a French university, and his thesis was on the subject of smallpox.

baa960da-cbd1-54e0-9d5e-f5269a2ff7f6.name: *Al-Maktab al-I‘dadiyya al-‘Askariyya, Damascus*
baa960da-cbd1-54e0-9d5e-f5269a2ff7f6.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum, State Museums
baa960da-cbd1-54e0-9d5e-f5269a2ff7f6.author: Stefan Weber
baa960da-cbd1-54e0-9d5e-f5269a2ff7f6.second_name: Military college founded first in 1830 in the Mamluk mosque of Tankiz
baa960da-cbd1-54e0-9d5e-f5269a2ff7f6.description2: Attempts were first made by the Ottoman state to reform schools in 1869 with the passing of an edict on school reform for the whole Ottoman Empire, officially recognizing private and foreign schools while setting out the basic principles of state education. The law now made a distinction between schools preparing children for a civil service or administrative career on the one hand, and military schools on the other hand. Military primary and secondary schools were established, an example for the latter is the significant Military College al-Maktab al-I‘dadiyya al-`Askariyya.

bae5f080-ad41-5249-82bc-b0f3de4d1129.name: *Médailles d'honneur d'or et de 1er mérite* \[…\] Biberon-Robert, flexible, patented \[…\] Only the very best doesn't let your child go thirsty
bae5f080-ad41-5249-82bc-b0f3de4d1129.description2: As infant mortality was still commonplace in the 19th century, the need to instil young parents with an understanding of hygiene in order to counter child illness quickly became clear. This poster advertises a new child's feeding bottle, showcasing its high quality and foregrounding an image of a healthy baby.

bd9ac0b4-17dd-5d2a-86a5-baadbae9f621.name: Jeweller’s tools box
bd9ac0b4-17dd-5d2a-86a5-baadbae9f621.holder: Jordan Folklore Museum, Department of Antiquities
bd9ac0b4-17dd-5d2a-86a5-baadbae9f621.author: Huda Kilani
bd9ac0b4-17dd-5d2a-86a5-baadbae9f621.description2: Jeweller’s wooden box to keep tools such as hand drills, punctures and screws, and soldering iron clumps. This tool box belonged to an Armenian jeweller whose family left their country during the First World War and settled in Jerusalem. The jeweller then moved to Amman and settled there in 1948. The Armenians were well known as skilled craftsmen and jewellers. The owner of this box worked as a jeweller since the 1950's, using his tool box until his death. The tool box demonstrates the relationship between different waves of migration and the variegated demographic composition of the Jordanians.

bde2bde2-7481-545c-9b6c-11a32b97be4d.name: Hôpital Habib-Thameur
bde2bde2-7481-545c-9b6c-11a32b97be4d.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
bde2bde2-7481-545c-9b6c-11a32b97be4d.history: This hospital, built in 1891 in the el-Halfaouine quarter by a group of Italian doctors, was initially called l'Hôpital Colonial Italien de Tunis and served the Italian residents of the city, most of which had emigrated from Sicily. It was moved to the building of the current Hôpital Habib-Thameur on the 15 March 1900, and in 1907 was renamed l'Hôpital Giuseppe Garibaldi, after the famous hero of Italian independence. Upon the arrival of English troops on 7 January 1943 it became a French hospital, and was renamed again to l'Hôpital de la Libération on the 6 June of the following year. It was finally given its current name by the Tunisian government following independence, in honour of the great doctor and militant nationalist Habib Thameur.
bde2bde2-7481-545c-9b6c-11a32b97be4d.keywords: Hospital; Charles Nicolle; Giuseppe Garibaldi; Habib Thameur
bde2bde2-7481-545c-9b6c-11a32b97be4d.description2: This hospital, which was constantly being expanded and renovated, started off with 150 beds. The hospital was served by Italian doctors, who were quickly joined by French doctors, and provided general medical services, as well as surgery, internal medicine, ophthalmology and radiology. Like the Hôpital Charles Nicolle, it also became prestigious university hospital following Tunisian independence.

bf87a0de-3e3f-504b-8bbb-757c5d6c17a8.name: *Faculty of Medicine Sports Teams at the Egyptian University*
bf87a0de-3e3f-504b-8bbb-757c5d6c17a8.keywords: Education; Students; Student Sports; Student Teams; Faculty of Medicine; Egyptian University
bf87a0de-3e3f-504b-8bbb-757c5d6c17a8.description2: The first sports teams at Egyptian University's Faculty of Medicine, where students achieved many regional and international victories. The 1923 Constitution stipulated that “Primary education is mandatory for all Egyptian boys and girls”. A decree was issued for the establishment of a public university under the name “The Egyptian University” in 1925, comprised of four faculties; literature, science, medicine and law. Ever since its establishment, the University has paid great attention to sport and university sport teams.

bfd5d0b7-c555-5670-8bef-67d8e0f7c0a2.name: Primary students at a village school in central Italy, which followed the teaching methods introduced by Maria Montessori
bfd5d0b7-c555-5670-8bef-67d8e0f7c0a2.author: Giulia Barrera
bfd5d0b7-c555-5670-8bef-67d8e0f7c0a2.archival: Collezione tessile di Tela Umbra, Fondo fotografico
bfd5d0b7-c555-5670-8bef-67d8e0f7c0a2.description2:
When Italy became a nation state in 1861, the illiteracy rate in the country was 78 per cent. In 1901, it was still at 56 per cent. Illiteracy was particularly high in the countryside. In 1877, the “Coppino Law”, made elementary schools mandatory and free of charge.  
Maria Montessori (1870-1952) was a medical doctor who developed innovative teaching methods for primary-school children. Her educational methods were first applied during the first decade of the 20th century. They met with great success and were applied in thousands of schools all over Europe and North America.

c0d03656-54de-5836-824e-12905a80c7a5.name: Coffee grinder
c0d03656-54de-5836-824e-12905a80c7a5.holder: Jordan Folklore Museum, Departmant of Antiquities
c0d03656-54de-5836-824e-12905a80c7a5.author: Huda Kilani
c0d03656-54de-5836-824e-12905a80c7a5.keywords: coffee; coffee grinding; coffee beans; domestic furnishing; domestic vessels
c0d03656-54de-5836-824e-12905a80c7a5.description2: Manual coffee grinder carved out of a hard wood, usually oak. The grinder consists of two parts: the mortar and the pestle. The mortar is highly decorated with floral and geometric designs. After roasting the coffee beans, the local Bedouins use these to grind the beans. The sound of grinding functions as an invitation to others to come and chat while enjoying freshly prepared coffee.

c0d68bf3-fc29-5afb-9f0b-b36ef1a39350.name: "Workers' pensions"
c0d68bf3-fc29-5afb-9f0b-b36ef1a39350.keywords: Precarity; workers; pensions; elections; cartoon; caricature
c0d68bf3-fc29-5afb-9f0b-b36ef1a39350.description2: In 1910, a new law on "workers and farmers' pensions" introduced a compulsory insurance scheme. Before this, however, life was very different and many workers lived a very difficult old age, without financial support. The question of workers and farmers' pensions was one of the key electoral questions of the time therefore, as it concerned the majority of the population and those in power feared the social unrest it could trigger. This comical drawing mocks Alexandre Millerand (1859–1943), a socialist politician who forgot all his promises as soon as the elections were over.

c0fa2286-c49d-5054-a7e8-e9736fe3a90e.name: Flag of a workers’ league bearing the sign
c0fa2286-c49d-5054-a7e8-e9736fe3a90e.dates: Unknown (probably immediately after World War I)
c0fa2286-c49d-5054-a7e8-e9736fe3a90e.author: Giulia Barrera
c0fa2286-c49d-5054-a7e8-e9736fe3a90e.archival: ACS, Partito nazionale fascista, Mostra della Rivoluzione fascista
c0fa2286-c49d-5054-a7e8-e9736fe3a90e.description2:
This flag presumably belonged to a league of navvies, or labourers. It shows the tools used by workers employed in road construction, i.e. pickaxe and shovel.  
Starting from the last decades of the XIX century, trade unionism flourished in Italy. In the 1890s, in many towns different unions started to reunite in general unions at a town level, known as Camere del Lavoro (labour unions, modelled on the French Bourse du Travail). In 1906 the Confederazione Generale del Lavoro (CGdL), a national confederation of trade unions, was founded.

en: Centro studi Piero Gobetti, *Un' altra Italia nelle bandiere dei lavoratori: simboli e cultura dall'unità d'Italia all'avvento del fascismo*, Turin: Centro studi Piero Gobetti, 1980.

c1679a4a-eb18-5ec1-bd6f-8c176785d5ff.name: Pendant
c1679a4a-eb18-5ec1-bd6f-8c176785d5ff.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
c1679a4a-eb18-5ec1-bd6f-8c176785d5ff.author: Huda Kilani
c1679a4a-eb18-5ec1-bd6f-8c176785d5ff.keywords: triangle; silver; blue beads; Ottoman coins
c1679a4a-eb18-5ec1-bd6f-8c176785d5ff.description2: A thin silver triangular pendant and welded decoration with blue glass beads. Five chains dangle with Ottoman coins at the end. This kind of jewellery was part of the dowry the groom gave to the bride. Dowries consisted mostly of silver jewellery because only the rich could afford gold jewellery. The use of coins as pieces of jewellery, worn by brides in front of their relatives and friends, was an indirect statement of the financial status of the groom.

c16fad3d-de00-51aa-b32f-c08f9761a3dc.name: *Madame X*
c16fad3d-de00-51aa-b32f-c08f9761a3dc.keywords: Painting; Halil Pasha; orientalist Turkish painters
c16fad3d-de00-51aa-b32f-c08f9761a3dc.description2: The basis of Turkish painting drawing influence from western tradition was laid when *Mühendishane-i Berr-i Hümayun* (the Naval Academy) opened in 1795. Halil Pasha was foremost among the painters with a military background who founded a western-style art tradition in Turkey. He worked with Jean Leon Gerome in his atelier in Paris. He provided a unique distinction to the analysis of impressionist light and colour, and was an example of artists dealing with impressionist technique. Because of his qualified knowledge about anatomy and his interest in depicting the human figure, Halil Pasha had a unique place in Turkish Art History.

c1f0fcfc-f45c-5523-b9e1-39924bd50073.name: Class photograph in Jbeil
c1f0fcfc-f45c-5523-b9e1-39924bd50073.author: Hala Masri
c1f0fcfc-f45c-5523-b9e1-39924bd50073.description2: This photograph was taken in Smar Jbeil, a village in the Mount Lebanon district. The sign behind the children reads "*Vive L'Académie*."

c3807cee-a0e6-57d1-823b-3455f5db9857.author: Hala Masri
c3807cee-a0e6-57d1-823b-3455f5db9857.keywords: education; students; pupils; children; France; village
c3807cee-a0e6-57d1-823b-3455f5db9857.description2: This photograph was taken in Chahtoul, a village in Lebanon in the Keserwan district. The wooden board on the back reads "*Vive La France Chahtoul Liban* (Long Live France Chahtoul Lebanon).

c4179abe-6375-58e2-9109-f22b4b9e5ebd.name: Photograph: *Arabic School, Learning the Koran, Egypt*
c4179abe-6375-58e2-9109-f22b4b9e5ebd.description:
Stereoscopic photography that creates the illusion of depth of field from two apparently identical images mounted on a rigid board by using a specific viewfinder, or stereoscope.  
The arrival of Islam to Africa caused the birth of schools where the Qu'ran was taught in Arabic. Probably Islamic education was the first education system introduced in African populations. Islam establishes education as a key priority for children.  
Universities, *madrasas* (organised institutions with different levels for studying Islamic religion), and Qur'anic schools (first education that children receive) are used by Islam as educational institutions and have played an important role in spreading Islamic religious, social, moral and cultural values between African populations.  
In the *madrasas* and Qur'anic schools, the Qur'an is learned and memorised by reading and writing at a wooden table. The memorization of the Qur'an is done by copying the teacher a text written on paper, and later recited aloud until memorised. Students were not allowed to pass to another passage until the current passage had been memorized.
c4179abe-6375-58e2-9109-f22b4b9e5ebd.keywords: Photography; education; Egypt; scenes of life

c4322598-8028-5f79-ae2e-c4ce254ee9ee.name: Military Infirmary
c4322598-8028-5f79-ae2e-c4ce254ee9ee.description: This hospital (or *hastahane* in Ottoman Turkish), commissioned by Sultan 'Abd al-'Aziz (Abdülaziz) (1861-76) in 1865, was often referred to as the military infirmary. The building included two wings, and the northern wing housed a drugstore (*ajzah*). The courthouse which later inhabited the building was moved to a different location when it became the Lebanese University's Institute of Fine Arts.
c4322598-8028-5f79-ae2e-c4ce254ee9ee.author: Hady El Hajj, Jennifer Harb, Cynthia Karaki
c4322598-8028-5f79-ae2e-c4ce254ee9ee.history: In 1865, this military hospital was commissioned by the Ottoman sultan 'Abd al-'Aziz (Abdülaziz).The hospital was later converted to a courthouse by the French, who took control of the city in 1918 following the collapse of the Ottoman Empire. Today, the building houses the Lebanese University's Institute of Fine Arts.
c4322598-8028-5f79-ae2e-c4ce254ee9ee.keywords: Infirmary; Sultan Abdul Aziz; Military; Hospital

c64f3835-f9f7-5723-9b30-b413f5f0111c.name: *Homarus hakelensis* Fraas 1878 and clupeomorph fishes
c64f3835-f9f7-5723-9b30-b413f5f0111c.holder: National Museum of Natural History and Science (MUHNAC) / Museums of the University of Lisbon
c64f3835-f9f7-5723-9b30-b413f5f0111c.author: Liliana Póvoas (MUHNAC-UL), Pedro Dantas (MUHNAC-UL)
c64f3835-f9f7-5723-9b30-b413f5f0111c.keywords: Homarus hakelensis; clupeomorphs; Upper Cretaceous; lithographic limestone; National Museum of Natural History and Science; University of Lisbon
c64f3835-f9f7-5723-9b30-b413f5f0111c.description2: *Homarus* is as genus of marine crustacean decapode (lobster). Its first pair of legs is transformed into big claws showing dimorphism (one specialised into a crushing claw and the other into a cutting claw). In the fossil register we can find about eight species of Homarus. But nowadays only two exist: *Homarus gammarus* (European lobster) and *Homarus americanus* (American lobster). *Homarus hakelensis* is a fossil species described from specimens found at the Upper Cretaceous (Cenomanian) site of Hakel, Lebanon. In this plate we can also find some specimens of clupeomorph fishes. In this group of teleosts, that date back to the Early Cretaceous (c. 140 million years) belongs, today, the herring, the sardine and the anchovy, for example. They are generally small silvery marine fishes.
c64f3835-f9f7-5723-9b30-b413f5f0111c.holding_institution_org: Museu Nacional da Historia Natural e da Ciencia (MUHNAC)

c7278b24-cf58-5191-9342-586e5560d4ff.name: *Mlle. Lauta, first* \[French\] *woman to get a degree in philosophy*
c7278b24-cf58-5191-9342-586e5560d4ff.description2: Léontine Zanta (not Lauta, as indicated by the photograph) was the first French woman to receive a literature degree (not a philosophy degree), writing her thesis on revival of Stoicism in the 16th century. A journalist, teacher and novelist, she was also very interested in feminism.

c7423aea-5979-55f8-8902-e38b1ba58ec7.name: Photograph of a classroom at a traditional Qur'anic school
c7423aea-5979-55f8-8902-e38b1ba58ec7.description: In 1914, the French Protectorate put forward a new policy to modernise the education system in Morocco. Integrating the new policy with the traditional education system, scholars (the *'ulama´*) of al-Qarawiyyin University modernised educational material while still respecting the old system.

c783fc3a-6b1b-58c1-83a4-ba0e00d74936.description2: Pictured here are schoolteacher teaching his young pupil to write.

c7f58b8f-d101-5a99-a3cc-dcb898bbfeeb.name: An Algerian woman grinds her meal in an old wooden mill
c7f58b8f-d101-5a99-a3cc-dcb898bbfeeb.description2: Many Western photographers took great interest in women's daily lives, or in daily rural tasks. In this photograph from 1920 an Algerian woman is pictured as she grinds wheat with a wooden pestle and mortar.

c99f4a2d-2d4c-538b-b57e-e1ba93984854.name: *Votes for Women*
c99f4a2d-2d4c-538b-b57e-e1ba93984854.author: Victoria and Albert Museum
c99f4a2d-2d4c-538b-b57e-e1ba93984854.artist: Artist: Alfred Pearse; publisher: The Women's Press; printer: Spottiswoode, Dixon & Hunting Ltd
c99f4a2d-2d4c-538b-b57e-e1ba93984854.keywords: Women; equality; George; poster; suffragette; print; politics; propaganda; printing
c99f4a2d-2d4c-538b-b57e-e1ba93984854.materials: Paper, lithographic ink; colour lithograph on paper, planographic printing
c99f4a2d-2d4c-538b-b57e-e1ba93984854.description2:
This Suffragette poster was created in response to the Liberal Prime Minister Herbert Asquith's suppression of the 1910 Conciliation Bill, which proposed extending the vote in Britain and Ireland to around one million wealthy, property-owning women. It shows King George V painting the text 'We Bow to the Will of the People' onto a poster, whilst a man paints on the King's back, and a Suffragette paints onto the man’s. The cartoon aimed to show how Asquith had gone against the will of Parliament, the elected representatives of the people. The Suffragettes urged male voters to register their protest by voting against Liberal candidates in the next election.  
  
This poster was published by the Woman's Press, who oversaw the publishing and propaganda for the Suffragettes. It was designed by Alfred Pearse, under the pseudonym ‘A. Patriot', Pearse was a dedicated Suffragette supporter and designed many of their posters.

ca59fd60-c057-5dbf-a2fa-484dcab24b97.name: Ring
ca59fd60-c057-5dbf-a2fa-484dcab24b97.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
ca59fd60-c057-5dbf-a2fa-484dcab24b97.author: Huda Kilani
ca59fd60-c057-5dbf-a2fa-484dcab24b97.description2: Thin silver ring with oval-shaped agate stone set in silver with inherent decoration on the soundings. Silver jewellery was the most common, because only rich people could afford gold jewellery. The dowry of silver and gold jewellery was given by the groom to the bride, reflecting the financial status of the groom. The Jordanian economy relied on trades and crafts and new waves of people started to come to Jordan and began to settle for this purpose. This object is an example of how traditional fashion reflected the variegated population composition of Jordan in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It is also an example of local personal attire, fashion, costumes and rites.

ca84a358-0e08-5345-bc08-43570cf84e04.keywords: Women; stereograph; stereoscope; agriculture; peasants; work; Egypt; Sinai; grain; grinder; topography; photographs
ca84a358-0e08-5345-bc08-43570cf84e04.description2: Many of the most popular subjects of stereographs were of topographical views or of scenes unfamiliar to the western audience for whom they were generally produced. This group of Islamic women from Egypt's Sinai Peninsula is shown grinding corn. Their faces are hidden by veils. The veil turns away the gaze while at the same time attracting it. The secrecy of the veil prompted fascination for what was often seen as the mysterious and exotic world of the East or the 'Orient' to 19th-century western viewers. In contrast, the men in the background confront the camera.

cc3b74af-a7c4-51db-b788-69489a7072e4.author: Marina Minozzi
cc3b74af-a7c4-51db-b788-69489a7072e4.keywords: Italian sculptors; realism; Positivism; Verismo; social topics; post-unitarian Italian society; health; work; rights of workers; peasant; agriculture; working class; social changes; reforms; life expectancy; poverty; literacy; illiteracy; labour
cc3b74af-a7c4-51db-b788-69489a7072e4.copyright: Copyright image: Soprintendenza alla Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Moderna e Contemporanea.
cc3b74af-a7c4-51db-b788-69489a7072e4.description2: In 1880 Achille D’Orsi submitted two artworks, including *Proximus Tuus*, to the National Exhibition of Fine Arts in Brera. The sculpture of *Proximus Tuus* made D’Orsi famous as a member of the Italian “Verismo” school of painting. The misery and harshness of fieldwork is represented for the first time in sculpture to denounce the consequences of the brutalisation of the human beings. This clear social denunciation created the emergence of a huge debate over this issue. The body and the facial expression of the peasant exhausted by labour became a symbol of the working class. The sculpture makes a plea for sympathy and pity for the worker right from the work’s title, expressed in Latin. The subject of the painting has been reproduced and copied several times in order to produce greater awareness over these problems.

cc3eb98f-be74-5f38-85da-465d5c36d52e.description2: A rectangular piece of Syrian silk cloth (*atlas*) with a small piece of coloured cotton cloth on the front on two sides. There is a line of Ottoman coins sewn together with three tassels dangling at the end with different stones. Silver was the most common jewellery, given by the groom to the bride as dowry. The use of Ottoman coins as pieces of jewellery – shown by women to friends and relatives – was an indirect reference to the financial status of their husbands. Silk was imported from Syria. Its trade in the Syro-Palestinian area was common because of the lack of geographical and political boundaries; some cities were like twins because of their close proximity and exchange of trade goods and business.

d320c5a3-16a0-5b02-8130-8a58ce2b34cb.author: Hala Masri
d320c5a3-16a0-5b02-8130-8a58ce2b34cb.history:
Each confession in Lebanon worked on spreading its beliefs and principals. Therefore, religiously based educational institutions were built. In this case the catholic Greek Church inaugurated the Patriarchal College in 1865, and still exists nowadays.  
Many religious education institutions were built in Lebanon, a multi-confessional country, with the aim of spreading the beliefs and principles of the respective confession. This Patriarchal College was inaugurated by the Catholic Greek church in 1865 and is still in use today.
d320c5a3-16a0-5b02-8130-8a58ce2b34cb.description2:
During his reign Gregory founded both the Patriarchal College in Beirut in 1865 and the Patriarchal College in Damascus in 1875 and re-opened the Melkite seminary of 'Ayn Traz in 1866. A western kind of architecture with balconies and balustrades.  
Gregory II Youssef founded the Patriarchal College in Beirut in 1865 as well as the Patriarchal College in Damascus in 1875 and re-opened the Melkit seminary of 'Ayn Trez in 1866. The college was built in a Western style, as seen by the use of balconies and balustrades.

d3ddaba2-605a-593a-84dc-d55cd6a60174.description2: These finger guards are known as khabt (pl. khabta). They were an essential part of a pearl-diver's equipment, as they protected his finger tips from the sharp oyster shells and other unexpected dangerous objects the pearl-diver might brush his fingers against while searching the murky seabed. Much of his work had to rely on touch, as visibility was minimal and few dangers could be anticipated by sight alone. When not used, the finger guards were kept in a container filled with water to keep them supple.

d8f09c37-b8cb-56c1-917a-f069f4830ef2.description2: The position of governess was one of the few professions open to middle-class women of modest means, but it was often a lonely and difficult life because the social status of a governess was ambiguous. She was not a servant in the usual sense but nor was she on equal terms with the family who employed her. Here, the young woman holds a letter which has obviously stirred memories of home. It may be news of a death in her family - letters or cards with black borders were used to announce deaths. Redgrave had a personal interest in representing the life of a governess: his sister Jane was a governess and died young.

dbf4dc13-3f6b-5da9-bf05-cfabe7876ad3.description2: A silver circular disk with inherent decorations in the carving, and prominent dome above; chains dangling with oval shapes at the end. With two different length. This ornament was placed on the top of a high hat worn by al-Druze (Druse) women. Silver was the most common jewellery. The dowry of silver and gold jewellery was given by the groom to the bride, reflecting the financial status of the groom. This object illustrates the variegated social composition and the demographic changes in the Jordanian territory in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The al-Druze tribes migrated from Syria (Hawran) to north east Jordan in the early twentieth century because of their support for the Syrian revolution against the French occupation.

ddd75581-2e37-5baa-8483-63c54f368af5.description2: Long black silk dress (*malas*), narrow at the waist, wide at the bottom, embroidered with cross-stitch dark blue and red on the chest and on the front side, worn by women of the al-Druze tribes, with a shirt underneath. This object illustrates the variegated composition and the demographic changes of the Jordan population in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It also shows how the different populations brought with them their fashion, costumes and rites which contributed to the multifaceted social and cultural heritage of Jordan. The al-Druze tribes migrated from Syria (Hawran) to northeast Jordan in the early twentieth century because of their support for the Syrian revolution against the French occupation.

deb4b3a7-5e57-5235-b533-346c36e88be2.name: *Mahmud II, Sultan of Turkey* (1784–1839)
deb4b3a7-5e57-5235-b533-346c36e88be2.keywords: Mahmud II, Sultan of Turkey; Egypt; Janissary; Konya; Ibrahim Pasha; Muhammad Ali; Greece
deb4b3a7-5e57-5235-b533-346c36e88be2.description2:
Portrait of Mahmud II, Sultan of Turkey (1784–1839). In 1826 Mahmud II initiated the development of a modern army. This led to the uprising of the Janissary, which was quelled by massacring the rebellious troops. Under Mahmud II's reign, in 1821 the Greeks started their fight for freedom which was granted to them in the Peace of Adrianople in 1829.  
After the destruction of the Janissary, the Ottoman Empire under Sultan Mahmud II had only 35,000 badly trained regular soldiers in 1827. Due to the weakness of the Ottoman Empire, Ibrahim Pasha, the son of Muhammad 'Ali (ruler of Egypt), invaded Syria. On 20 February 1832, the Egyptian Army defeated the Ottoman Army at the Battle of Konya. This forced Mahmud II to sign the Peace of Kütahya and to cede Syria and Kilikia to Egypt.

dfd2eeea-301b-506a-85f9-f9ad927ce8f2.description2: Women's costumes of the central regions of Jordan are characterized by length, dark colours, light vertical strips of embroidery and very long sleeves. This black and blue dress has a very loose fitting, open chest and long flared sleeves pulled over a head band. The length of the dress was adjusted to the height of the woman by a sash. Wide at the bottom, it is decorated horizontally with blue cotton stripes and vertically with embroidery lines and Ottoman coins. The traditional costumes reflect the variegated population composition and demographic changes of the late 19th century-early 20th century Jordanian territory, when new waves of people arrived and settled for the purpose of trades and crafts. Craft was not limited to the everyday life and the profits from crafts were a source of income.

The rababa is played with a bow consisting of an arched stick with horse hair. The rababa is a musical instrument widely used in the Bedouin tradition. Music played in communal setting is an essential part of the traditions in Bedouin communities for leisure at communal gatherings.

e24c667e-3e74-52ad-9357-51224ea2c3d0.name: A letter from the Hashemite court
e24c667e-3e74-52ad-9357-51224ea2c3d0.description: A letter from the Hashemite court signed by al-Hussein bin 'Ali, the king of Arab countries and Sharif of Mecca. The letter was sent to the princes Faisal and al-Aziz al-Jarba, from Umm al-Qura (Mecca) in Rajab, 18th, AH 1336 / AD 1917 asking them to take care of Jacobean Armenian confession and to help them and to protect them as they protect themselves, their fortune and their sons. It says also to facilitate what they need either in their stay or travel, because they are free non-Muslims enjoying Muslim protection. Those are people who prophet Muhammad makes his will to take care of, and the one who doesn’t do so will be his (Muhammad's) adversary till Judgment Day. King Hussein says: this is one of the most important orders we ask you to do. He ends his letter by praying to God to grant the Emirs to do what he asks them.

e69b13bf-d0c7-5ed7-8570-ac7defc7d2a4.keywords: Women; work; Crimean war; politics; hygiene; hospitals; travel; traveller; science; medicine; surgery; nurse
e69b13bf-d0c7-5ed7-8570-ac7defc7d2a4.description2: Frances Margaret Taylor converted to the Roman Catholic faith from Anglicanism and founded the order of the Poor Servants of the Mother of God. In *Eastern Hospitals and English Nurses* (1856) she describes her experience as a nurse, prior to her conversion, in the hospitals of Scutari and Koulali, during the Crimean War, with Florence Nightingale. In addition to her personal experience, the book gives an account of medical and sanitary conditions, voluntary service and nursing, one of the few volunteering and job opportunities available to British women in the 19th century. The Crimean War carried nurses outside the boundaries of their country. The book highlights how their support was crucial in the organisation of medical activity and living conditions in the British military hospitals in Turkey and Crimea.

e8fc4581-ee8f-583c-a11e-54b1e44bda1a.description2: Padded bag to hold three small brass bottles of Arab eye-liner, perfumes and essential oils. It was used as a wall decoration. Decorated with silk tassels, glass beads, Egyptian and Ottoman coins. The Jordanian economy relied on trades and crafts and new waves of people started to settle in the Jordanian territory for these purposes. This object is an example of how traditional fashion reflected the variegated population composition of the area in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It is also an example of local personal attire, fashion, costumes and rites.

e9467b9f-6942-5d4d-ad65-2a08497b1ca5.description2: The Majlis of Ibrahim ibn Muhammad al-Midfa' is one of the very few remaining buildings in Sharjah dating back to the turn of the 14th/ 20th century. A traditional, now carefully restored, courtyard house, its unique feature is its circular *barjeel* or wind tower, the only one in the United Arab Emirates. Ibrahim ibn Muhammad al-Midfa', was a prominent cultural and intellectual personality in Sharjah. A keen observer and commentator on local and pan-Arab affairs, al-Midfa' transformed his majlis into a hub of intellectual activity and culture. The first ever newspaper in the UAE, entitled ‘Oman’, was published by him in 1927.

He specialized in dermatology in Gureba Hospital in Istanbul. This medical box belonged to Dr. İbrahim Ethem Göze is rectangular in shape, brown and covered with leather. It also has a handle for carrying. It is in two pieces with four chambers inside. One of the chambers has a cover. In the front there are salvarsan (Arsphenamine) medicine boxes used to cure syphilis, in the chamber at the back there are brown bottles on which sulphur, ammonia, alcohol and tincture of iodine is written. In the covered chamber there are ampules, bandage, a metal syringe with its needle and one tongue holder. On the box one can read the figure of 152.

ecc37fb3-5606-5413-bfb4-48ac62d9c763.second_name: *One of the Wards of the Hospital at Scutari*
ecc37fb3-5606-5413-bfb4-48ac62d9c763.description2: Florence Nightingale (1820–1910), a British nurse famous for her commitment to and improvement of the health service, was sent to on a humanitarian mission to Scutari in the middle of the Crimean war. With a team of about 30 nurses, she cleaned the hospital and reorganised the wards in order to prevent the outbreak of epidemics. In this image she is pictured in the sick ward, taking various measures to improve its hygiene.

eee2b270-70d5-58ca-a544-89ca4bbc9d54.name: *Armenian Girl*
eee2b270-70d5-58ca-a544-89ca4bbc9d54.description2: *Armenian Girl* by Frederick Lewis, and important orientalist painter and etcher.

f0667100-6159-569b-9a0e-84fec1b968f0.name: Headdress
f0667100-6159-569b-9a0e-84fec1b968f0.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
f0667100-6159-569b-9a0e-84fec1b968f0.author: Huda Kilani
f0667100-6159-569b-9a0e-84fec1b968f0.keywords: Ottoman; Russian coins; pendent; red and green silk
f0667100-6159-569b-9a0e-84fec1b968f0.materials: Silver, fabric, glass beads, coins; casting, welding, weaving
f0667100-6159-569b-9a0e-84fec1b968f0.description2: Three bands of silver chain fitted around the sides and over the crown of the head and attached to a surrounding fabric patterned in minute beadwork and sewn with various Ottoman and Russian coins. From this head-piece hangs a long piece of cotton sewn with coins of the Ottoman Empire with a rectangular pendant and multiple red and green silk tassels on the back. Headdresses like this one were worn by married women, as silver was the most common jewellery. The dowry of silver and gold jewellery was given by the groom to the bride. The Ottoman and Russian coins reflect the social and economic situation of Jordan between the end of the 19th century and the early 20th century, when it was part of the Ottoman empire and it was influenced by population movements, demographic changes and trade with distant countries.

f1e6ba55-3ae0-5ba0-9651-a37492696a21.name: The Syrian independence movement; a crowd protesting in the streets of Damascus
f1e6ba55-3ae0-5ba0-9651-a37492696a21.description2: A feminist movement emerged in French mandate Syria (1920–1946), which aimed to obtain, among other things, the right to vote. Some protesters can be seen in this photograph, which was taken during an independence rally in Damascus.

f3955418-aaed-57fc-96f9-18195a4d076b.name: *Atik Valide Mosque*
f3955418-aaed-57fc-96f9-18195a4d076b.keywords: Painting; Hüseyin Zekai Pasha; orientalist Turkish painters
f3955418-aaed-57fc-96f9-18195a4d076b.description2: The majority of Turkish painters in the 19th century were Ottoman officers who had studied abroad. Hüseyin Zekai Pasha was one of those painters. Following his education at the Kuleli Military High School, he continued his studies at the Military Academy (*Mektebi Harbiye*), where he had a chance to learn technical drawing and perspective. His first period was realistic and his pictorial representation includes scenes or events from everyday life. In his first works, Hüseyin Zekai Pasha followed the painting tradition of 19th century, including thin paint dough and light colours. He made changes in his techniques through the Galatasaray Exhibition and eventually he turned into an impressionist whose work was dominated by thicker brush strokes.

f398bf92-d6b1-56a3-bb47-793d5811643e.name: Models of traditional agricultural environment in Egypt and Sudan and the life in the Egyptian oases at Fu`ad Agricultural Museum
f398bf92-d6b1-56a3-bb47-793d5811643e.dates: 16 January 1938 (Photos taken during the inauguration of the museum)
f398bf92-d6b1-56a3-bb47-793d5811643e.description2: The Fu`ad Agriculture Museum was considered the first of its kind in the Middle East and the Arab World during the 1930s. It was inaugurated during the time of King Faruq, the son of King Fu`ad, and houses a large number of collections related to agricultural and rural environments, as well as agricultural plants and animals.

f5a5076a-5db4-51ca-8079-bb3a7252511c.name: Bronze standard
f5a5076a-5db4-51ca-8079-bb3a7252511c.author: Aida Naghawi
f5a5076a-5db4-51ca-8079-bb3a7252511c.keywords: Bronze; standard; palace gate; Hussein I
f5a5076a-5db4-51ca-8079-bb3a7252511c.description2: A bronze standard in form of a royal crown rested on a glob where a phrase: "a wish for long life to king", date AH 1350 / AD 1931, is incised. There are two holes on the base indicates how it was fixed on a post. The standard used to be hold by a guard in front of the palace gate, it belongs to king Hussein I 1853–1931.

f5bf8d60-ea7d-51ea-b865-00084437d439.name: A strike of rice weeders in northern Italy: the women on strike try to stop a train carrying workers hired by the landowners to replace them

f5bf8d60-ea7d-51ea-b865-00084437d439.description2: Women were very active in trade unions. In 1906, a woman, Argentina Altobelli, became secretary general of the National Federation of Agricultural Workers (Federazione nazionale dei lavoratori della terra).
